item.title: JavaScript Introduction
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
HTML gives a page structure and CSS makes it look good. JavaScript makes it do things: respond to clicks, check forms, load new data without reloading, show and hide menus, run games. It's the only programming language that runs natively in every web browser, which makes it one of the most useful languages you can learn.

Your first JavaScript

console.log("Hello, world!");
console.log(2 + 3);

Click Try it Yourself and press Run. You'll see Hello, world! and 5 in the output. console.log() prints a value to the console, a panel developers use to see what their code is doing. You'll use it in almost every lesson.

JavaScript changes the page

Here's JavaScript working with HTML:

<h2 id="greeting">Hello!</h2>
<button id="btn">Click me</button>

<script>
  const button = document.getElementById("btn");
  const heading = document.getElementById("greeting");

  button.addEventListener("click", function () {
    heading.textContent = "You clicked the button!";
  });
</script>

Click the button and the heading changes. In three steps, the script:

  1. Finds the button and the heading on the page.
  2. Waits for a click on the button.
  3. Changes the heading's text when the click happens.

Almost every interactive feature on the web follows this pattern: find elements, listen for something, change something.

HTML, CSS and JavaScript together

What JavaScript can do

In the browser:

  • React to clicks, typing, scrolling and other events.
  • Change any HTML or CSS on the page.
  • Check form input before it's sent.
  • Load data from servers (weather, search results, new posts) without reloading.
  • Save small amounts of data in the browser, e.g. a dark-mode preference.
  • Draw graphics and run games.

Outside the browser, with Node.js, JavaScript also runs web servers, command-line tools and desktop apps. Learn it once and use it nearly everywhere.

JavaScript is not Java

Despite the name, JavaScript has nothing to do with Java. The name was a marketing decision in 1995. The official standard is called ECMAScript; "ES6" or "ES2015" refers to a big update that added modern features like let, const and arrow functions, which you'll learn in this course.

A taste of the language

let name = "Asha";
let age = 21;

if (age >= 18) {
  console.log(name + " is an adult.");
} else {
  console.log(name + " is a minor.");
}

for (let i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  console.log("Counting: " + i);
}

Don't worry about understanding every line yet. You'll learn variables, if statements and loops step by step. Notice that it reads almost like English.

Statements and semicolons

A JavaScript program is a list of statements, instructions run from top to bottom. Each one usually ends with a semicolon ;. JavaScript can often add missing semicolons automatically, but writing them yourself avoids rare, confusing bugs. This course always uses them.

Comments

// A single-line comment

/*
  A comment that
  spans several lines
*/

console.log("Comments are ignored when the code runs.");

Case sensitivity

JavaScript is case-sensitive: name, Name and NAME are three different things, and console.Log() (capital L) is an error. When something doesn't work, check the capitalisation first.

How to practise

  • Use Try it Yourself on every example in this course and change things.
  • In any browser, press F12 (or Ctrl + Shift + J) and open the Console tab. You can type JavaScript there and press Enter to run it immediately.
  • Make mistakes on purpose and read the error messages. Learning to read errors is half of programming.

Common mistakes

  • Wrong capitalisation: Console.log or getElementByID.
  • Missing quotes around text: console.log(Hello) looks for a variable called Hello.
  • Mismatched brackets ( ) and braces { }.
  • Smart quotes pasted from a word processor (“ ”) instead of plain quotes (" ").

Exercise

  1. Print your name and your favourite food with two console.log() lines.
  2. Print the result of 7 * 6.
  3. In the button example, change the new heading text to something of your own.
  4. Open your browser's console on any website and type 2 ** 10. What do you get?

Summary

  • JavaScript adds behaviour to web pages and also runs on servers with Node.js.
  • console.log() prints values so you can see what your code does.
  • Interactive features follow the pattern: find elements, listen for events, change the page.
  • JavaScript is case-sensitive, and statements end with semicolons.

Next, you'll learn where to put JavaScript in an HTML page.
item.excerpt:encoded: What JavaScript is, what it can do in the browser and beyond, how it relates to HTML and CSS, and your first lines of code.

item.title: Where to Put JavaScript
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Just like CSS, JavaScript can live inside the HTML page or in a separate file. Where and how you load it affects whether it works at all, and how fast your page appears.

Inline script element

The simplest way is a <script> element with code inside it:

<p id="msg">Waiting…</p>

<script>
  document.getElementById("msg").textContent = "JavaScript is running!";
</script>

The browser reads the page from top to bottom. When it reaches <script>, it stops, runs the code, and then continues.

Why order matters

A script can only find elements that the browser has already read. This fails:

<script>
  // The paragraph doesn't exist yet when this runs
  const p = document.getElementById("late");
  console.log(p); // null
</script>

<p id="late">I come after the script.</p>

getElementById returns null ("nothing"), and trying to change null causes an error. That's why scripts used to be placed at the end of the body, after all the HTML:

<body>
  <h1>My page</h1>
  <p id="intro">Hello</p>

  <script>
    document.getElementById("intro").textContent = "Found it!";
  </script>
</body>

External JavaScript files

On real websites, JavaScript goes in its own file, for example js/main.js:

// js/main.js
console.log("main.js loaded");

Link it with the src attribute:

<script src="js/main.js"></script>
  • A <script> with src must be empty; any code between the tags is ignored.
  • The closing </script> tag is required.

Benefits are the same as for external CSS: one file shared by every page, cached by the browser, and clean HTML.

defer: the modern best practice

Put the script in the <head> with the defer attribute:

<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>My page</title>
  <script src="js/main.js" defer></script>
</head>

defer tells the browser:

  1. Download the file in the background while reading the HTML (no pause).
  2. Run it only after the whole page has been read, so every element exists.
  3. Run several deferred scripts in the order they appear.

This gives you the best of both: the download starts early, and your code can safely find any element. Use defer for almost all your scripts.

async

<script src="https://example.com/analytics.js" async></script>

async also downloads in the background, but runs the script as soon as it arrives, possibly before the page is finished and in any order. It's for independent scripts that don't touch your page's elements, such as analytics or ads.

The DOMContentLoaded event

If you must use a script in the head without defer (for example, inline code), wait for the page to be ready:

<script>
  document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", function () {
    document.getElementById("box").textContent = "The page is ready.";
  });
</script>
<p id="box">Loading…</p>

The code inside runs once the whole HTML has been read.

JavaScript modules

Modern code is often split into modules that import from each other:

<script type="module" src="js/app.js"></script>

Module scripts are deferred automatically and can use import and export. You'll meet them later; for now, defer is all you need.

Inline event attributes (avoid)

Old tutorials often show this:

<button onclick="alert('Hi!')">Old style</button>

It works, but mixing code into HTML is hard to maintain and blocked by strict security settings. Use addEventListener in your script instead, as you'll learn in the Events lesson.

Common mistakes

  • Script before the elements it uses, without defer: null errors.
  • **Code inside a <script src="…">**, which is silently ignored.
  • Wrong file path in src. Check the console and Network tab (F12) for a 404 error.
  • **Forgetting </script>**: <script src="x.js" /> is not valid.

Exercise

  1. Make a page with a paragraph and an inline script at the end of the body that changes its text.
  2. Move the script into main.js, link it in the head without defer, and see the error in the console.
  3. Add defer and check that it works again.
  4. Add console.log("one") in one deferred file and console.log("two") in a second; confirm the order.

Summary

  • JavaScript goes in <script> elements or external .js files linked with src.
  • Scripts can only find elements the browser has already read.
  • Use <script src="…" defer> in the head: it downloads early and runs when the page is ready.
  • Use async only for independent scripts like analytics.

Next, you'll learn the different ways to show output from JavaScript.

item.title: JavaScript Output (console.log)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A program is only useful if you can see what it's doing. JavaScript can show output in several places: the developer console, the web page itself, and pop-up dialogs. Each has its own job.

console.log(): your best friend

console.log("Hello");
console.log(42);
console.log(true);
console.log("Total:", 19.99, "INR");

console.log() prints to the browser's console. You can pass several values separated by commas, and they're printed with spaces between them.

Developers use it constantly to check what's happening: "What's in this variable right now?" "Did this part of the code even run?" It's invisible to normal visitors, so it doesn't affect the page.

Logging objects and arrays

const user = { name: "Asha", age: 21, skills: ["HTML", "CSS"] };
console.log(user);

const scores = [92, 87, 95];
console.log(scores);

The console shows the whole structure, which is very handy when working with data. In the browser's own console you can click to expand nested values.

Other console methods

console.info("Information");
console.warn("Careful: this looks wrong");
console.error("Something broke");

console.table([
  { language: "HTML", lessons: 20 },
  { language: "CSS", lessons: 20 },
  { language: "JavaScript", lessons: 25 }
]);
  • console.warn and console.error are shown in yellow and red in the browser console and are easy to filter.
  • console.table displays an array of objects as a neat table (open your browser's console with F12 to see it).

Template literals: easier messages

Joining text with + gets messy. Template literals use backticks (`) and ${ } to insert values:

const name = "Rohan";
const lessons = 7;

console.log("Hi " + name + ", you finished " + lessons + " lessons.");
console.log(`Hi ${name}, you finished ${lessons} lessons.`);
console.log(`Next lesson number: ${lessons + 1}`);

Both lines print the same thing, but the second is much easier to read and write. You can put any expression inside ${ }. You'll use template literals throughout the course.

Writing into the page

To show output to visitors, change an element's content:

<p id="result"></p>

<script>
  const price = 499;
  const qty = 3;
  document.getElementById("result").textContent = `Total: ₹${price * qty}`;
</script>

textContent sets the text inside an element. There's also innerHTML, which interprets the string as HTML:

<div id="box"></div>

<script>
  document.getElementById("box").innerHTML = "<strong>Bold</strong> and <em>italic</em>";
</script>

**Be careful with innerHTML:** never put text typed by users into it. If a user types <img src=x onerror=...>, the browser runs it as code, a security hole called cross-site scripting (XSS). Use textContent for plain text, which is always safe.

alert, confirm and prompt

<button id="a">Alert</button>
<button id="c">Confirm</button>
<button id="p">Prompt</button>

<script>
  document.getElementById("a").addEventListener("click", function () {
    alert("This is an alert.");
  });
  document.getElementById("c").addEventListener("click", function () {
    const ok = confirm("Delete this item?");
    console.log("User chose:", ok);
  });
  document.getElementById("p").addEventListener("click", function () {
    const name = prompt("What's your name?");
    console.log("Name entered:", name);
  });
</script>
  • alert() shows a message with an OK button.
  • confirm() asks OK/Cancel and returns true or false.
  • prompt() asks for text and returns it (or null if cancelled).

These are handy for quick tests, but they block the whole page and look different in every browser. Real websites use custom dialogs built with HTML and CSS.

document.write (avoid)

You may see document.write("Hello") in old tutorials. If it runs after the page has loaded, it erases the whole page. Don't use it.

Debugging with the console

When something doesn't work:

  1. Open the console (F12 → Console).
  2. Look for red error messages. They tell you what went wrong and on which line. Click the file name to jump to the line.
  3. Add console.log() lines to check values step by step.
const items = ["pen", "book"];
console.log("items is:", items);
console.log("first item:", items[0]);
console.log("third item:", items[2]); // undefined: there's no third item

Common mistakes

  • Expecting visitors to see console.log: it's for developers. Use textContent for visitors.
  • **Using innerHTML with user input**, creating a security hole.
  • Regular quotes instead of backticks in template literals: "Hi ${name}" prints the ${name} literally.
  • Leaving lots of console.log calls in finished code. Clean up before publishing.

Exercise

  1. Store your name and age in two variables and print a sentence with a template literal.
  2. Print an array of three friends with console.log and an array of objects with console.table (in your browser console).
  3. Create a page that shows "2 + 2 = 4" inside a paragraph, calculated by JavaScript.
  4. Add a button that uses confirm() and writes "Confirmed" or "Cancelled" into the page.

Summary

  • console.log() prints values for developers; warn, error and table add variety.
  • Template literals (`Hi ${name}`) make messages easy.
  • textContent safely shows text to visitors; use innerHTML only with trusted HTML.
  • alert, confirm and prompt are quick tests, not real UI.

Next, you'll store values in variables with let and const.
item.excerpt:encoded: Show results with console.log and its relatives, write into the page with textContent, use alert sparingly, and debug with the browser console.

item.title: JavaScript Variables (let and const)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A variable is a named box that stores a value so you can use it later: a user's name, a score, a list of products. Variables are the most basic building block of every program.

Declaring a variable with let

let score = 0;
console.log(score); // 0

score = 10;
console.log(score); // 10

score = score + 5;
console.log(score); // 15
  • let creates (declares) a variable.
  • = assigns a value. In programming, = doesn't mean "equals"; it means "put this value into the box".
  • After declaring a let variable, you can change its value as often as you like.

score = score + 5 reads as: take the current value of score, add 5, and store the result back in score.

Constants with const

const siteName = "VitalStack";
const pi = 3.14159;

console.log(siteName, pi);

// siteName = "Other"; // TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.

const creates a variable that can't be reassigned. Try uncommenting the last line: it causes an error.

Which one to use?

**Use const by default.** Switch to let only when you know the value will change (a counter, a running total, a variable updated in a loop). This makes code easier to understand: when you see const, you know that name always refers to the same value.

const taxRate = 0.18;     // never changes
let total = 0;            // will change

total = total + 100;
total = total + 250;
console.log(`Total with tax: ${total * (1 + taxRate)}`);

const with arrays and objects

const stops you from reassigning the variable, but the contents of an array or object can still change:

const cart = ["pen"];
cart.push("notebook");     // allowed: changing the contents
console.log(cart);         // ["pen", "notebook"]

// cart = ["eraser"];      // error: reassigning the variable

Declaring without a value

let username;
console.log(username); // undefined

username = "rohan_k";
console.log(username);

A variable declared without a value holds undefined. A const must be given a value immediately.

Several variables at once

let x = 1, y = 2, z = 3;
console.log(x + y + z);

This works, but one declaration per line is easier to read.

Naming rules

Names can contain letters, digits, _ and $, but:

  • Can't start with a digit: 1st is invalid, first is fine.
  • Can't contain spaces or hyphens: user-name is invalid.
  • Can't be a reserved word like let, if, function or class.
  • Are case-sensitive: total and Total are different.

Naming conventions

JavaScript developers use camelCase: start lowercase, capitalise each following word.

let firstName = "Meera";
let totalPrice = 1299;
let isLoggedIn = true;
const MAX_UPLOAD_MB = 10; // fixed configuration values are often UPPER_CASE

Choose names that say what the value is: price beats p, userEmails beats arr. Booleans read well with is, has or can: isOpen, hasAccess.

Swapping and updating values

let a = "first";
let b = "second";

let temp = a;
a = b;
b = temp;

console.log(a, b); // "second" "first"

let count = 5;
count += 2;  // same as count = count + 2
count -= 1;  // count = count - 1
count++;     // add 1
console.log(count); // 7

The old var keyword

Before 2015, JavaScript only had var. You'll see it in older code:

var oldStyle = "still works";
console.log(oldStyle);

var has confusing behaviour: it ignores block boundaries like if and for, and can be used before it's declared without an error. let and const fixed these problems. **Don't use var in new code.** You'll understand the details in the Scope lesson.

Common mistakes

  • **Reassigning a const** → TypeError: Assignment to constant variable.
  • **Declaring the same let twice** in the same block → SyntaxError: Identifier has already been declared. Declare once, then assign without let.
  • Using a variable before declaring it → ReferenceError.
  • Meaningless names like x1, data2, temp3 in real code.

Exercise

  1. Create const variables for your name and birth year, and a let for the current year. Print your age.
  2. Create let balance = 1000. Subtract a purchase of 250 with -= and add a refund of 50 with +=. Print the result.
  3. Swap the values of two variables using a third one.
  4. Try reassigning a const and read the error message in the output.

Summary

  • Variables store values; = assigns a value.
  • Use const by default, and let when the value must change.
  • Name variables in camelCase with descriptive names.
  • Avoid var in new code.

Next, you'll learn the different types of data a variable can hold.
item.excerpt:encoded: Store values in variables with let and const, learn naming rules, when to use each keyword, and why to avoid the old var.

item.title: JavaScript Data Types
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Every value in JavaScript has a type: text is a string, 42 is a number, true is a boolean. The type decides what you can do with a value: you can multiply numbers but not sentences. Understanding types helps you avoid some of JavaScript's most famous surprises.

The main types

const name = "Asha";             // string
const age = 21;                  // number
const price = 199.5;             // number (no separate decimal type)
const isStudent = true;          // boolean
let nickname;                    // undefined
const middleName = null;         // null
const user = { name: "Asha" };   // object
const skills = ["HTML", "CSS"];  // array (a kind of object)

console.log(typeof name, typeof age, typeof isStudent);

JavaScript has seven primitive types (string, number, boolean, undefined, null, bigint, symbol) plus objects. You'll use the first five and objects every day; bigint and symbol are for special cases.

Strings

Text, written in quotes:

const single = 'Hello';
const double = "Hello";
const template = `Hello, ${single}!`;
console.log(single, double, template);

Single and double quotes work the same. Backticks create template literals with ${ } placeholders. Strings get a whole lesson of their own.

Numbers

console.log(10 + 5);      // 15
console.log(7 / 2);       // 3.5
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);   // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(10 / 0);      // Infinity
console.log("abc" * 2);   // NaN
  • Whole numbers and decimals are the same type.
  • 0.1 + 0.2 isn't exactly 0.3 because of how computers store decimals. For money, calculate in the smallest unit (paise, cents) or round the result.
  • NaN means "Not a Number": the result of a maths operation that makes no sense.

Booleans

Only two values: true and false. They're the answers to yes/no questions and drive every decision in a program:

const age = 20;
const isAdult = age >= 18;
console.log(isAdult); // true

undefined and null

Both mean "no value", with a small difference:

  • undefined: a value hasn't been set yet. JavaScript uses it automatically: an unassigned variable, a missing object property, a function that returns nothing.
  • null: intentionally empty. You set it yourself to say "there's deliberately nothing here".
let selectedCourse;
console.log(selectedCourse); // undefined: not chosen yet

let winner = null;           // we know there's no winner yet
console.log(winner);

Objects and arrays

Objects group related values under names; arrays hold ordered lists:

const book = { title: "Clean Code", pages: 464, available: true };
const colours = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(book.title);   // "Clean Code"
console.log(colours[0]);   // "red"

Both have full lessons later in this course.

Checking a type with typeof

console.log(typeof "hi");        // "string"
console.log(typeof 3.14);        // "number"
console.log(typeof false);       // "boolean"
console.log(typeof undefined);   // "undefined"
console.log(typeof {});          // "object"
console.log(typeof []);          // "object" (arrays are objects)
console.log(typeof null);        // "object" (a famous old bug!)
console.log(Array.isArray([]));  // true: the right way to check for arrays

typeof null returning "object" is a mistake from 1995 that can never be fixed without breaking old websites. To check for null, use value === null.

Dynamic typing

A variable can hold any type, and the type can change:

let value = 42;
console.log(typeof value); // "number"
value = "forty-two";
console.log(typeof value); // "string"

This is flexible but can hide bugs. (TypeScript, a popular extension of JavaScript, adds type checking for big projects.)

Type conversion

JavaScript often converts types automatically, sometimes surprisingly:

console.log("5" + 2);   // "52": + with a string joins text
console.log("5" - 2);   // 3: - only works on numbers, so "5" becomes 5
console.log("5" * "2"); // 10
console.log(true + 1);  // 2: true becomes 1

The + rule causes the most bugs: values from form fields are always strings, so "10" + "5" gives "105", not 15.

Convert explicitly to be safe:

const input = "10";
console.log(Number(input) + 5);   // 15
console.log(String(99) + "%");    // "99%"
console.log(parseInt("42px"));    // 42
console.log(parseFloat("3.5kg")); // 3.5
console.log(Number("hello"));     // NaN

Truthy and falsy

In conditions, every value counts as either true or false. These are falsy:

// false, 0, "" (empty string), null, undefined, NaN
console.log(Boolean(0), Boolean(""), Boolean(null));  // false false false
console.log(Boolean("0"), Boolean([]), Boolean("hi")); // true true true

Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false" and empty arrays. You'll use this in if statements: if (username) { ... } runs only when username isn't empty.

Common mistakes

  • Adding form values without converting: "10" + "5" → "105".
  • Checking arrays with typeof instead of Array.isArray().
  • Exact comparisons of decimals like 0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3 (false).
  • **Confusing null and undefined**; check for both with value == null or explicitly.

Exercise

  1. Create one variable of each main type and print each with its typeof.
  2. Predict the result of "3" + 4 + 5 and 3 + 4 + "5", then check. (Hint: JavaScript works left to right.)
  3. Convert the string "250" to a number and add 50.
  4. Print Boolean() of 0, "0", [], "" and "hello".

Summary

  • Main types: string, number, boolean, undefined, null, object (including arrays).
  • typeof checks a type; use Array.isArray() for arrays and === null for null.
  • + with a string joins text; convert with Number(), String(), parseInt().
  • Falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy.

Next, you'll learn operators for maths, comparison and logic.
item.excerpt:encoded: Strings, numbers, booleans, undefined, null, objects and arrays; checking types with typeof; and how JavaScript converts between types.

item.title: JavaScript Operators
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Operators are the symbols that do work on values: + adds, > compares, && combines conditions. You've already used a few. This lesson covers all the everyday operators, plus one rule that prevents many bugs: always use ===.

Arithmetic operators

console.log(10 + 3);  // 13  addition
console.log(10 - 3);  // 7   subtraction
console.log(10 * 3);  // 30  multiplication
console.log(10 / 3);  // 3.3333333333333335  division
console.log(10 % 3);  // 1   remainder (modulo)
console.log(2 ** 5);  // 32  exponent (2 to the power 5)

The remainder operator % is more useful than it looks:

const n = 14;
console.log(n % 2 === 0 ? "even" : "odd"); // even
console.log(125 % 60); // 5: 125 seconds is 2 minutes and 5 seconds

Order of operations

Like in maths, *, / and % happen before + and -. Use brackets to make the order clear:

console.log(2 + 3 * 4);   // 14
console.log((2 + 3) * 4); // 20

Increment and decrement

let likes = 10;
likes++;    // 11
likes--;    // 10
console.log(likes);

Assignment operators

let total = 100;
total += 50;  // total = total + 50  → 150
total -= 20;  // total = total - 20  → 130
total *= 2;   // total = total * 2   → 260
total /= 4;   // total = total / 4   → 65
console.log(total);

let greeting = "Hello";
greeting += ", world";
console.log(greeting); // "Hello, world"

Comparison operators

Comparisons produce a boolean, true or false:

console.log(5 > 3);    // true
console.log(5 < 3);    // false
console.log(5 >= 5);   // true
console.log(4 <= 3);   // false
console.log(5 === 5);  // true  equal
console.log(5 !== 3);  // true  not equal

=== vs ==: always use the triple version

console.log(5 == "5");    // true: == converts types before comparing
console.log(5 === "5");   // false: === also checks the type
console.log(0 == "");     // true (!)
console.log(0 === "");    // false
console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false

== ("loose equality") converts values to the same type first, which leads to strange results like 0 == "" being true. === ("strict equality") compares value and type, with no surprises.

**Rule: use === and !== everywhere.** If you need to compare a form value with a number, convert it first: Number(input) === 5.

Comparing strings

console.log("apple" < "banana"); // true: alphabetical order
console.log("Zebra" < "apple");  // true: uppercase letters come before lowercase!
console.log("10" < "9");         // true: compared as text, character by character

Strings are compared character by character using their character codes. To compare numbers stored as text, convert them first.

Logical operators

const age = 25;
const hasTicket = true;

console.log(age >= 18 && hasTicket);  // AND: true only if both are true
console.log(age < 12 || age > 60);    // OR: true if at least one is true
console.log(!hasTicket);              // NOT: flips true/false

Short-circuiting

&& and || stop as soon as they know the answer, and return one of the actual values (not always true/false):

const name = "";
console.log(name || "Guest");          // "Guest": || returns the first truthy value

const user = { name: "Asha" };
console.log(user && user.name);        // "Asha": && returns the last value if all are truthy

value || "default" is a classic way to provide a fallback.

Nullish coalescing (??)

|| treats 0 and "" as missing, which is sometimes wrong:

const savedVolume = 0;
console.log(savedVolume || 50);  // 50: wrong, the user chose 0!
console.log(savedVolume ?? 50);  // 0: ?? only falls back on null or undefined

Use ?? when 0, "" or false are valid values.

The ternary operator

A compact if/else that produces a value:

const score = 72;
const result = score >= 40 ? "Pass" : "Fail";
console.log(result); // "Pass"

condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse. Great for simple choices; use a real if statement for anything longer.

typeof and other operators

You've met typeof. Two more you'll see later: in (does an object have a property?) and instanceof (was an object made from a certain class?).

Common mistakes

  • **Using = in a comparison**: if (x = 5) assigns 5 instead of comparing. Use ===.
  • **Using ==** and getting surprising true results.
  • Comparing numeric strings like "10" < "9".
  • **Using || for defaults** when 0 or "" are valid; use ??.

Exercise

  1. Write code that prints whether 37 is even or odd using %.
  2. Convert 200 minutes into hours and minutes with /, Math.floor() and %.
  3. Given age and hasId, print whether someone can enter a club (18+ and has ID).
  4. Use a ternary to print "Free shipping" if a cart total is 500 or more, otherwise "Add more items".
  5. Compare 0 || 10 with 0 ?? 10 and explain the difference.

Summary

  • Arithmetic: + - * / % **; assignment shortcuts: += -= *= /= ++ --.
  • Comparisons return booleans. **Always use === and !==.**
  • &&, || and ! combine conditions; || and ?? provide defaults.
  • condition ? a : b chooses between two values.

Next, you'll work with text using strings and their methods.
item.excerpt:encoded: Arithmetic, assignment, comparison and logical operators, why to use === instead of ==, the ternary operator, and nullish coalescing.

item.title: JavaScript Strings
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Strings hold text: names, messages, URLs, whole articles. Because so much of web development is about text, JavaScript gives strings many built-in methods, ready-made functions that work on them.

Creating strings

const a = "double quotes";
const b = 'single quotes';
const c = `backticks: ${a.length} characters in a`;
console.log(a, b, c);

If your text contains one kind of quote, wrap it in the other, or escape it with a backslash:

const s1 = "It's easy";
const s2 = 'She said "hi"';
const s3 = 'It\'s also fine';
const s4 = "Line one\nLine two"; // \n is a new line
console.log(s1, s2, s3);
console.log(s4);

Template literals can span several lines directly:

const card = `Name: Asha
Course: JavaScript
Lesson: 7`;
console.log(card);

Length and characters

const word = "VitalStack";
console.log(word.length);        // 10
console.log(word[0]);            // "V": the first character is at index 0
console.log(word[word.length - 1]); // "k": the last character
console.log(word.at(-1));        // "k": at() accepts negative positions

Positions (indexes) start at 0, not 1. This is true for strings and arrays throughout JavaScript.

Strings are immutable: you can't change one character in place. Methods always return a new string.

Changing case and trimming

const email = "  Asha@Example.COM  ";
console.log(email.trim());               // "Asha@Example.COM"
console.log(email.trim().toLowerCase()); // "asha@example.com"
console.log("hello".toUpperCase());      // "HELLO"

trim() removes spaces from both ends, essential for cleaning form input. trimStart() and trimEnd() remove from one side.

Notice you can chain methods: each returns a new string, and the next method works on that.

Searching

const sentence = "Learn JavaScript at VitalStack";

console.log(sentence.includes("Java"));    // true
console.log(sentence.startsWith("Learn")); // true
console.log(sentence.endsWith("Stack"));   // true
console.log(sentence.indexOf("at"));       // 17: position of the first match
console.log(sentence.indexOf("Python"));   // -1: not found

Searches are case-sensitive. To search without caring about case, lower-case both sides:

const search = "javascript";
console.log(sentence.toLowerCase().includes(search.toLowerCase())); // true

Extracting parts with slice

const text = "JavaScript";
console.log(text.slice(0, 4));  // "Java": from index 0 up to (not including) 4
console.log(text.slice(4));     // "Script": from 4 to the end
console.log(text.slice(-6));    // "Script": the last 6 characters

slice(start, end) is the main method for cutting strings. (substring is similar; you'll see it in older code.)

Replacing

const msg = "I like cats. cats are great.";
console.log(msg.replace("cats", "dogs"));    // replaces the first match only
console.log(msg.replaceAll("cats", "dogs")); // replaces every match

Splitting and joining

const csv = "HTML,CSS,JavaScript";
const parts = csv.split(",");
console.log(parts);              // ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"]
console.log(parts.join(" | "));  // "HTML | CSS | JavaScript"

const letters = "hello".split("");
console.log(letters);            // ["h", "e", "l", "l", "o"]
console.log(letters.reverse().join("")); // "olleh"

split turns a string into an array; join turns an array back into a string. Together they solve many text problems.

Padding and repeating

console.log("7".padStart(3, "0"));  // "007"
console.log("5".padStart(2, "0") + ":" + "3".padStart(2, "0")); // "05:03"
console.log("=".repeat(20));

padStart is perfect for formatting times, dates and invoice numbers.

A practical example: making a URL slug

function slugify(title) {
  return title
    .trim()
    .toLowerCase()
    .replaceAll(" ", "-");
}

console.log(slugify("  JavaScript Strings Explained ")); // "javascript-strings-explained"

(You'll learn functions properly in lesson 15. For now, notice how chaining makes each step clear.)

Comparing strings

console.log("abc" === "abc");     // true
console.log("abc" === "ABC");     // false
console.log("ä".localeCompare("z", "de")); // -1: sorts correctly for languages

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting indexes start at 0: the first character is str[0].
  • Expecting methods to change the original: name.toUpperCase() returns a new string; save it: name = name.toUpperCase().
  • Case-sensitive searches that miss matches.
  • **Using replace when you meant replaceAll.**

Exercise

  1. Take " hello WORLD " and turn it into "Hello world" (trim, lower-case, then capitalise the first letter with slice).
  2. Check if an email address contains @ and ends with .com.
  3. Count the words in a sentence with split(" ") and .length.
  4. Reverse any word and check whether it's a palindrome (like "level").
  5. Format the time 9:5 as "09:05" with padStart.

Summary

  • Create strings with quotes or backticks; escape quotes with \.
  • length and [index] read strings; indexes start at 0; strings never change in place.
  • Key methods: trim, toLowerCase, includes, indexOf, slice, replaceAll, split, padStart.
  • Chain methods to do several steps in one readable expression.

Next, you'll work with numbers and the Math object.
item.excerpt:encoded: Create and combine strings, read characters, and use the essential string methods to search, slice, change case, trim, split and replace text.

item.title: JavaScript Numbers
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Numbers are everywhere in programs: prices, scores, sizes, timers. JavaScript has a single number type for both whole numbers and decimals, plus a built-in Math object full of useful functions.

Integers and decimals

const items = 3;          // integer
const price = 249.99;     // decimal (floating point)
const big = 1_000_000;    // underscores make big numbers readable
console.log(items * price, big);

The decimal precision problem

console.log(0.1 + 0.2);            // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);    // false

Computers store decimals in binary, and some decimals (like 0.1) can't be stored exactly. It's the same in Python, Java and most languages. Two solutions:

// 1. Round when displaying
console.log((0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2));  // "0.30"

// 2. For money, calculate in the smallest unit (paise, cents)
const pricePaise = 24999;     // ₹249.99
const totalPaise = pricePaise * 3;
console.log(totalPaise / 100); // 749.97

Rounding

const n = 4.567;
console.log(Math.round(n));  // 5: nearest whole number
console.log(Math.floor(n));  // 4: always down
console.log(Math.ceil(n));   // 5: always up
console.log(Math.trunc(-4.7)); // -4: just removes the decimals
console.log(n.toFixed(1));   // "4.6": a string with 1 decimal

toFixed() returns a string, which is perfect for display. Convert back with Number() if you need to calculate further.

Math.ceil is handy for page counts: 23 items at 10 per page needs Math.ceil(23 / 10) = 3 pages.

Converting strings to numbers

Values from form fields and URLs are always strings:

console.log(Number("42"));       // 42
console.log(Number("42.5"));     // 42.5
console.log(Number(""));         // 0 (careful!)
console.log(Number("42px"));     // NaN
console.log(parseInt("42px"));   // 42: reads digits until it hits something else
console.log(parseFloat("3.75 kg")); // 3.75
console.log(+"7");               // 7: the unary plus also converts
  • Number() is strict: the whole string must be a number.
  • parseInt() and parseFloat() read from the start and stop at the first invalid character.

NaN and checking for valid numbers

const result = Number("abc");
console.log(result);                 // NaN
console.log(result === NaN);         // false: NaN is not equal to anything, even itself!
console.log(Number.isNaN(result));   // true: the correct check
console.log(Number.isFinite(42));    // true
console.log(Number.isInteger(4.0));  // true
console.log(Number.isInteger(4.5));  // false

When validating user input, Number.isFinite(Number(value)) checks that it's a real, usable number.

The Math object

console.log(Math.max(4, 19, 7));   // 19
console.log(Math.min(4, 19, 7));   // 4
console.log(Math.abs(-12));        // 12: distance from zero
console.log(Math.sqrt(81));        // 9
console.log(Math.pow(2, 8));       // 256 (same as 2 ** 8)
console.log(Math.PI);              // 3.141592653589793

Math.max(...array) finds the largest value in an array (the ... "spread" operator is explained in the Arrays lessons):

const scores = [72, 95, 88];
console.log(Math.max(...scores)); // 95

Random numbers

Math.random() returns a decimal from 0 (included) up to 1 (not included):

console.log(Math.random());

// A whole number from 1 to 6, like a dice roll:
const dice = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;
console.log("You rolled", dice);

// Pick a random item from an array:
const tips = ["Drink water", "Take a break", "Stretch"];
console.log(tips[Math.floor(Math.random() * tips.length)]);

The pattern Math.floor(Math.random() * N) gives a whole number from 0 to N − 1. (Don't use Math.random() for passwords or security codes; browsers have crypto.getRandomValues() for that.)

Formatting numbers for people

const amount = 1234567.891;
console.log(amount.toLocaleString("en-IN"));  // "12,34,567.891"
console.log(amount.toLocaleString("en-US"));  // "1,234,567.891"

const inr = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", { style: "currency", currency: "INR" });
console.log(inr.format(249.5));    // "₹249.50"

const usd = new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" });
console.log(usd.format(249.5));    // "$249.50"

const pct = new Intl.NumberFormat("en", { style: "percent" });
console.log(pct.format(0.42));     // "42%"

Intl.NumberFormat formats numbers correctly for any country, including currency symbols and digit grouping (Indian lakhs and crores, or Western thousands).

Common mistakes

  • Comparing decimals exactly: round first or work in whole units.
  • **Checking x === NaN**: always false. Use Number.isNaN(x).
  • **Forgetting toFixed returns a string**: price.toFixed(2) + 1 joins text.
  • **Math.random() * 6 without Math.floor**, giving decimals.
  • **Number("") being 0**: check for empty input separately.

Exercise

  1. Calculate the total of 3 items at ₹199.90 and show it with exactly 2 decimals.
  2. Write code that rolls two dice and prints both values and their sum.
  3. Convert "1500.75" to a number, add 18% tax, and format it as Indian rupees.
  4. Calculate how many pages are needed to show 47 search results at 10 per page.
  5. Check whether the input "12abc" is a valid number with Number() and Number.isNaN().

Summary

  • JavaScript has one number type; decimals can be slightly imprecise, so round or use whole units.
  • Math.round, floor, ceil and toFixed handle rounding.
  • Number(), parseInt() and parseFloat() convert strings; check results with Number.isNaN.
  • Math.random() makes random numbers; Intl.NumberFormat formats them for people.

Next, you'll make decisions in your code with if and else.
item.excerpt:encoded: Work with numbers: rounding, fixed decimals, converting from strings, NaN checks, the Math object, random numbers and formatting prices.

item.title: JavaScript If/Else
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Programs need to make decisions: show a "Log in" button or the user's name, charge shipping or not, pass or fail a test. The if statement runs code only when a condition is true.

if

const temperature = 34;

if (temperature > 30) {
  console.log("It's hot. Drink water!");
}

console.log("This line always runs.");

The condition goes in brackets ( ). If it's true, the code inside the braces { } runs; if not, it's skipped.

else

const age = 16;

if (age >= 18) {
  console.log("You can vote.");
} else {
  console.log(`You can vote in ${18 - age} years.`);
}

Exactly one of the two blocks runs.

else if: more than two options

const score = 76;
let grade;

if (score >= 90) {
  grade = "A";
} else if (score >= 75) {
  grade = "B";
} else if (score >= 60) {
  grade = "C";
} else if (score >= 40) {
  grade = "D";
} else {
  grade = "F";
}

console.log(`Score ${score} → grade ${grade}`);

JavaScript checks the conditions from top to bottom and runs the first block whose condition is true, then skips the rest. That's why the order matters here: a score of 95 is also >= 75, but it never reaches that check because the first condition already matched.

Combining conditions

const age = 25;
const hasLicence = true;
const isWeekend = false;

if (age >= 18 && hasLicence) {
  console.log("You can rent a car.");
}

if (isWeekend || age < 12) {
  console.log("Discounted ticket.");
} else {
  console.log("Regular ticket.");
}

if (!hasLicence) {
  console.log("Apply for a licence first.");
}

Use brackets to make complex conditions clear: if ((a && b) || c).

Truthy checks

Because every value is truthy or falsy, you can check whether something "exists":

const username = "";

if (username) {
  console.log(`Welcome back, ${username}!`);
} else {
  console.log("Welcome, guest!");
}

const cart = [];
if (cart.length) {
  console.log("You have items in your cart.");
} else {
  console.log("Your cart is empty.");
}

Remember: an empty array [] is truthy, so check cart.length, not cart. And 0 is falsy, so if (count) is false when count is 0.

A real example: form validation

<form id="signup">
  <label for="pw">Password</label>
  <input id="pw" type="password">
  <button>Sign up</button>
  <p id="msg"></p>
</form>

<script>
  document.getElementById("signup").addEventListener("submit", function (event) {
    event.preventDefault();
    const pw = document.getElementById("pw").value;
    const msg = document.getElementById("msg");

    if (pw.length === 0) {
      msg.textContent = "Please enter a password.";
    } else if (pw.length < 8) {
      msg.textContent = "Use at least 8 characters.";
    } else if (!/[0-9]/.test(pw)) {
      msg.textContent = "Add at least one number.";
    } else {
      msg.textContent = "Looks good!";
    }
  });
</script>

Type different passwords and submit. (/[0-9]/.test(pw) checks for a digit using a regular expression; you don't need to understand it yet.)

Guard clauses: avoid deep nesting

Nested ifs quickly become hard to read:

function checkout(user, cart) {
  if (user) {
    if (cart.length > 0) {
      if (user.address) {
        return "Order placed!";
      } else {
        return "Add an address.";
      }
    } else {
      return "Cart is empty.";
    }
  } else {
    return "Please log in.";
  }
}
console.log(checkout({ address: "Pune" }, ["book"]));

The same logic with guard clauses handles the problem cases first and exits early:

function checkout(user, cart) {
  if (!user) return "Please log in.";
  if (cart.length === 0) return "Cart is empty.";
  if (!user.address) return "Add an address.";
  return "Order placed!";
}
console.log(checkout({ address: "Pune" }, []));

Flat, readable, and easy to extend. (You'll learn function and return in lesson 15.)

Ternary for simple choices

const isMember = true;
const price = isMember ? 199 : 299;
console.log(`Price: ₹${price}`);

Use the ternary for a quick choice between two values. Use if for anything that runs several statements.

Braces: always use them

JavaScript allows an if without braces for a single line:

const x = 5;
if (x > 3) console.log("big");

This is fine for very short guard clauses, but adding a second line later without adding braces is a classic bug. When in doubt, use braces.

Common mistakes

  • **= instead of ===** in the condition: if (x = 5) is always true.
  • **Wrong order of else if checks**, so a broad condition catches values meant for a later branch.
  • **Checking an empty array with if (arr)**, which is always true.
  • Semicolon after the condition: if (x > 3); { … } runs the block every time.

Exercise

  1. Given a number, print "positive", "negative" or "zero".
  2. Write a shipping calculator: free over ₹500, ₹40 under ₹500, and ₹0 for members whatever the total.
  3. Given an hour from 0–23, print "Good morning", "Good afternoon" or "Good evening".
  4. Rewrite a three-level nested if from your own code with guard clauses.

Summary

  • if (condition) { … } runs code only when the condition is true; else handles the rest.
  • else if chains are checked top to bottom; the first match wins.
  • Combine conditions with &&, || and !; use truthy checks carefully.
  • Guard clauses keep logic flat and readable.

Next, you'll learn the switch statement for choosing between many fixed values.
item.excerpt:encoded: Make decisions with if, else if and else, combine conditions, use truthy checks, write guard clauses and avoid deeply nested code.

item.title: JavaScript Switch
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
When you compare one value against many possible exact values, a long else if chain gets repetitive. The switch statement is designed for exactly this case.

Basic switch

const day = "tue";
let message;

switch (day) {
  case "mon":
    message = "Start of the week. Plan your lessons.";
    break;
  case "tue":
    message = "Tuesday: practise JavaScript.";
    break;
  case "wed":
    message = "Midweek review.";
    break;
  default:
    message = "Keep going!";
}

console.log(message);

How it works:

  1. The value in switch ( ) is compared with each case using strict equality (===).
  2. When a case matches, the code after it runs.
  3. break exits the switch.
  4. default runs if no case matches (like a final else).

The same logic with if/else

const day = "tue";
let message;

if (day === "mon") {
  message = "Start of the week. Plan your lessons.";
} else if (day === "tue") {
  message = "Tuesday: practise JavaScript.";
} else if (day === "wed") {
  message = "Midweek review.";
} else {
  message = "Keep going!";
}
console.log(message);

Both are correct. switch reads more clearly when there are many cases comparing the same value with fixed options.

Don't forget break: fall-through

Without break, execution "falls through" into the next case:

const level = 2;

switch (level) {
  case 1:
    console.log("Level 1 unlocked");
  case 2:
    console.log("Level 2 unlocked");
  case 3:
    console.log("Level 3 unlocked");
}
// Prints "Level 2 unlocked" and "Level 3 unlocked"

Once case 2 matches, every following case runs too, until a break or the end. Forgetting break is the most common switch bug.

Grouping cases on purpose

Fall-through is useful when several values should share the same code:

const month = 2;
let days;

switch (month) {
  case 2:
    days = 28;
    break;
  case 4:
  case 6:
  case 9:
  case 11:
    days = 30;
    break;
  default:
    days = 31;
}

console.log(`Month ${month} has ${days} days (ignoring leap years).`);

Empty cases stacked on top of each other all run the same block.

Switch uses strict comparison

const input = "1";

switch (input) {
  case 1:
    console.log("number one");
    break;
  case "1":
    console.log("string one");
    break;
}
// "string one": "1" !== 1

Values from forms are strings, so convert them (Number(input)) or use string cases.

Ranges with switch (true)

switch compares exact values, so ranges like "score above 90" are better written with if/else. You'll sometimes see this trick:

const score = 82;

switch (true) {
  case score >= 90:
    console.log("A");
    break;
  case score >= 75:
    console.log("B");
    break;
  default:
    console.log("C or below");
}

It works (each case expression is compared with true), but most developers find an if/else chain clearer for ranges.

Returning from switch inside a function

Inside a function, return exits immediately, so no break is needed:

function statusLabel(code) {
  switch (code) {
    case 200: return "OK";
    case 404: return "Not Found";
    case 500: return "Server Error";
    default:  return "Unknown status";
  }
}

console.log(statusLabel(404));
console.log(statusLabel(418));

An alternative: object lookup

For mapping values to values, an object is often shortest:

const labels = {
  200: "OK",
  404: "Not Found",
  500: "Server Error"
};

const code = 500;
console.log(labels[code] ?? "Unknown status");

You'll learn objects in lesson 14. Rule of thumb:

  • Object lookup: simple value → value mappings.
  • switch: each case needs to run different statements.
  • if/else: ranges and complex conditions.

Common mistakes

  • **Missing break**, causing accidental fall-through.
  • Type mismatch: case 1 won't match the string "1".
  • Using switch for ranges where if/else is clearer.
  • **Forgetting default** for unexpected values.

Exercise

  1. Write a switch that converts a number 1–7 into a day name, with a default "Invalid day".
  2. Group cases so that "sat" and "sun" print "Weekend" and other days print "Weekday".
  3. Write a simple calculator: given two numbers and an operator ("+", "-", "*", "/"), print the result.
  4. Rewrite your day-name switch as an object lookup.

Summary

  • switch compares one value against many case values with ===.
  • break stops execution; without it, code falls through to the next case.
  • Stack empty cases to share code; default handles everything else.
  • Use object lookups for simple mappings and if/else for ranges.

Next, you'll repeat code with for and while loops.
item.excerpt:encoded: Choose between many exact values with switch, understand break and fall-through, use default, and know when an object lookup is cleaner.

item.title: JavaScript Loops (for, while)
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Computers are great at repetition. A loop runs the same code many times: printing every item in a list, counting down a timer, trying a password until it's right. JavaScript has several loops; each suits a different situation.

The for loop

for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  console.log(`Lap ${i}`);
}

The brackets have three parts, separated by semicolons:

  1. Start: let i = 1 runs once, before the loop begins.
  2. Condition: i <= 5 is checked before each round. If false, the loop stops.
  3. Update: i++ runs after each round.

So the loop runs with i = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, then stops when i becomes 6.

Counting in other ways

for (let i = 10; i > 0; i -= 2) {
  console.log(i); // 10, 8, 6, 4, 2
}

// Times table
const n = 7;
for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  console.log(`${n} × ${i} = ${n * i}`);
}

Looping over an array by index

const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];

for (let i = 0; i < fruits.length; i++) {
  console.log(`${i + 1}. ${fruits[i]}`);
}

Indexes start at 0, so the condition is i < fruits.length (not <=).

for...of: the easy way to loop over values

const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];

for (const fruit of fruits) {
  console.log(fruit);
}

for (const letter of "Hi!") {
  console.log(letter);
}

for...of gives you each value directly: no index, no off-by-one errors. Use it whenever you don't need the index. It works on arrays, strings and other "iterable" collections.

while

A while loop repeats as long as a condition is true. Use it when you don't know in advance how many rounds you'll need:

let balance = 1000;
let months = 0;

while (balance < 2000) {
  balance = balance * 1.1; // 10% growth per month
  months++;
}

console.log(`It takes ${months} months to double: ${balance.toFixed(2)}`);

do...while

do...while checks the condition after each round, so the code always runs at least once:

let roll;
let attempts = 0;

do {
  roll = Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1;
  attempts++;
  console.log(`Rolled ${roll}`);
} while (roll !== 6);

console.log(`Got a 6 after ${attempts} attempts.`);

break and continue

  • break exits the loop immediately.
  • continue skips the rest of this round and moves on to the next.
const numbers = [4, 9, -1, 16, 25];

for (const n of numbers) {
  if (n < 0) {
    console.log("Negative number found, stopping.");
    break;
  }
  console.log(`√${n} = ${Math.sqrt(n)}`);
}

for (let i = 1; i <= 10; i++) {
  if (i % 3 === 0) continue; // skip multiples of 3
  console.log(i);
}

Looping over objects with for...in

const course = { title: "JavaScript", lessons: 25, level: "beginner" };

for (const key in course) {
  console.log(`${key}: ${course[key]}`);
}

for...in loops over an object's keys (property names). Don't use it on arrays; use for...of there. You'll also see Object.entries() in the Objects lesson, which is often nicer.

Nested loops

A loop inside a loop runs the inner loop completely for every round of the outer one:

for (let row = 1; row <= 3; row++) {
  let line = "";
  for (let col = 1; col <= 4; col++) {
    line += "* ";
  }
  console.log(line);
}

Nested loops are useful for grids and tables, but can get slow on large data: 1,000 × 1,000 is a million rounds.

Building results in a loop

A very common pattern: start with an empty value and add to it in each round.

const prices = [199, 349, 99, 520];
let total = 0;
let expensive = [];

for (const price of prices) {
  total += price;
  if (price > 300) {
    expensive.push(price);
  }
}

console.log(`Total: ₹${total}`);
console.log("Items over ₹300:", expensive);

In the Array Methods lesson you'll learn shortcuts like reduce and filter that do this in one line.

Infinite loops

If the condition never becomes false, the loop never stops and the page freezes:

// DON'T RUN THIS
// let i = 0;
// while (i < 5) {
//   console.log(i);   // i never changes, so i < 5 is always true
// }

Always make sure something inside the loop moves it towards its end. If a page freezes, close the tab.

Which loop to use

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one errors: i <= arr.length goes one past the end.
  • Forgetting to update the counter in a while loop → infinite loop.
  • **Using for...in on arrays**, which gives string indexes and can include extra properties.
  • Changing an array's length while looping over it.

Exercise

  1. Print all even numbers from 2 to 20.
  2. Sum the numbers from 1 to 100 (the answer is 5050).
  3. Given an array of names, print only names longer than 4 characters with for...of.
  4. Print a 5-row triangle of stars (*, **, ***…) with nested loops.
  5. Use a while loop to find how many times you can halve 1000 before it drops below 1.

Summary

  • for counts; for...of loops over values; for...in loops over object keys.
  • while repeats while a condition is true; do...while runs at least once.
  • break exits a loop; continue skips to the next round.
  • Make sure every loop can end.

Next, you'll learn arrays, the main way to store lists in JavaScript.

item.title: JavaScript Arrays
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
An array is an ordered list of values: a shopping list, the lessons in a course, the scores in a game. Arrays are one of the two data structures you'll use constantly in JavaScript (the other is objects).

Creating arrays

const languages = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"];
const scores = [92, 87, 95, 78];
const mixed = ["Asha", 21, true, null];
const empty = [];

console.log(languages);
console.log(scores.length); // 4

Square brackets, values separated by commas. An array can hold any mix of types, though in practice each array usually holds one kind of thing.

Reading items by index

const colours = ["red", "green", "blue"];

console.log(colours[0]);                  // "red": the first item
console.log(colours[2]);                  // "blue"
console.log(colours[colours.length - 1]); // "blue": the last item
console.log(colours.at(-1));              // "blue": at() supports negative indexes
console.log(colours[10]);                 // undefined: there's no item 10

The first item is at index 0, the last at length - 1.

Changing items

const week = ["Mon", "Tue", "Wed"];
week[1] = "Tuesday";
console.log(week); // ["Mon", "Tuesday", "Wed"]

Even with const, you can change what's inside an array; you just can't replace the whole array with a new one.

Adding and removing at the ends

const queue = ["Asha", "Rohan"];

queue.push("Meera");       // add to the end
console.log(queue);        // ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]

queue.unshift("Kabir");    // add to the start
console.log(queue);        // ["Kabir", "Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"]

const last = queue.pop();  // remove from the end
console.log(last, queue);  // "Meera" ["Kabir", "Asha", "Rohan"]

const first = queue.shift(); // remove from the start
console.log(first, queue);   // "Kabir" ["Asha", "Rohan"]

Adding and removing in the middle: splice

const tasks = ["wake up", "exercise", "breakfast", "study"];

tasks.splice(1, 1);                    // at index 1, remove 1 item
console.log(tasks);                    // ["wake up", "breakfast", "study"]

tasks.splice(2, 0, "shower");          // at index 2, remove 0, insert "shower"
console.log(tasks);                    // ["wake up", "breakfast", "shower", "study"]

tasks.splice(0, 1, "wake up early");   // replace the first item
console.log(tasks);

splice(start, deleteCount, ...itemsToInsert) changes the array in place.

Finding items

const tags = ["html", "css", "js", "css"];

console.log(tags.includes("js"));     // true
console.log(tags.indexOf("css"));     // 1: first position
console.log(tags.lastIndexOf("css")); // 3
console.log(tags.indexOf("python"));  // -1: not found

Slicing and joining arrays

const letters = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"];

console.log(letters.slice(1, 3)); // ["b", "c"]: copy from 1 up to (not including) 3
console.log(letters.slice(-2));   // ["d", "e"]
console.log(letters);             // unchanged

const more = letters.concat(["f", "g"]);
console.log(more);

console.log(letters.join("-"));   // "a-b-c-d-e"

slice makes a copy and doesn't change the original; splice changes the original. Their names are confusingly similar, so double-check which one you mean.

The spread operator

... "spreads" an array's items out. It's the modern way to copy and combine arrays:

const frontend = ["HTML", "CSS", "JavaScript"];
const backend = ["Python", "SQL"];

const fullStack = [...frontend, ...backend];
console.log(fullStack);

const copy = [...frontend];
copy.push("React");
console.log(frontend); // unchanged
console.log(copy);

Why copying matters

Arrays are stored by reference: assigning an array to another variable doesn't copy it.

const original = [1, 2, 3];
const sameArray = original;  // not a copy!
sameArray.push(4);
console.log(original);       // [1, 2, 3, 4]: changed too

Both names point to the same array. Use [...original] when you need an independent copy.

Destructuring

Pull values out of an array into variables:

const point = [10, 25];
const [x, y] = point;
console.log(x, y);

const [winner, runnerUp, ...others] = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera", "Kabir"];
console.log(winner, runnerUp, others);

Arrays of arrays

const board = [
  ["X", "O", "X"],
  ["O", "X", "O"],
  ["O", "X", "X"]
];
console.log(board[1][2]); // "O": row 1, column 2

Sorting

const names = ["Rohan", "asha", "Meera"];
names.sort();
console.log(names); // ["Meera", "Rohan", "asha"]: uppercase sorts first!

const nums = [10, 1, 5, 100];
nums.sort();
console.log(nums);  // [1, 10, 100, 5]: sorted as text!

nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);
console.log(nums);  // [1, 5, 10, 100]: numeric sort

By default, sort compares items as strings. For numbers, always pass a compare function (a, b) => a - b (you'll understand the arrow syntax in lesson 16). sort and reverse change the original array.

Common mistakes

  • Off-by-one: the last item is arr[arr.length - 1], not arr[arr.length].
  • Sorting numbers without a compare function.
  • **Thinking = copies an array**: use spread.
  • **Mixing up slice (copy) and splice (change).**

Exercise

  1. Create an array of five favourite films. Print the first, the last and the total count.
  2. Add one film to the start and one to the end; remove the third one with splice.
  3. Combine two arrays of friends with the spread operator.
  4. Sort [45, 3, 120, 7, 64] from smallest to largest.
  5. Use destructuring to get the first two items of an array and the rest separately.

Summary

  • Arrays are ordered lists; indexes start at 0; length gives the count.
  • push, pop, shift, unshift and splice add and remove items.
  • includes, indexOf, slice, concat and join search and copy.
  • Use spread [...arr] to copy or combine; sort numbers with (a, b) => a - b.

Next, you'll learn powerful array methods like map, filter and reduce.
item.excerpt:encoded: Store ordered lists in arrays: create them, read and change items by index, add and remove with push, pop, shift, unshift and splice, and copy with spread.

item.title: JavaScript Array Methods
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Most real programs work with lists of data: products, users, messages, lessons. JavaScript arrays have built-in methods that let you loop, transform, search and summarise lists in one line each. Learning these well will change how you write code.

All the methods in this lesson take a function as an argument, which is called once for each item. We'll write those functions with the short arrow syntax, item => something. You'll learn functions in detail in lessons 15 and 16; for now, read n => n * 2 as "take n, give back n times 2".

The sample data

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 1499, category: "electronics", inStock: false },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, category: "electronics", inStock: true },
  { name: "Backpack", price: 1899, category: "bags", inStock: true }
];
console.log(products.length, "products");

The examples below each start with a copy of this data so they run on their own.

forEach: do something with each item

const names = ["Asha", "Rohan", "Meera"];

names.forEach((name, index) => {
  console.log(`${index + 1}. ${name}`);
});

forEach simply runs the function for every item. It returns nothing. (for...of does the same job, and many developers prefer it.)

map: transform every item

map creates a new array of the same length, with each item transformed:

const prices = [120, 1499, 250];

const withTax = prices.map(p => Math.round(p * 1.18));
console.log(withTax); // [142, 1769, 295]

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120 },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250 }
];
const labels = products.map(p => `${p.name}: ₹${p.price}`);
console.log(labels);

Use map whenever you think "I want a list of X from this list of Y". It's how lists of data become lists of HTML elements on a page.

filter: keep only matching items

filter creates a new array with only the items for which the function returns true:

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, inStock: true },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 1499, inStock: false },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, inStock: true }
];

const available = products.filter(p => p.inStock);
console.log(available.map(p => p.name)); // ["Notebook", "USB cable"]

const cheap = products.filter(p => p.price < 300);
console.log(cheap.length); // 2

const numbers = [5, 12, 8, 21, 3];
console.log(numbers.filter(n => n % 2 === 0)); // [12, 8]

find and findIndex: the first match

const users = [
  { id: 1, name: "Asha" },
  { id: 2, name: "Rohan" },
  { id: 3, name: "Meera" }
];

const user = users.find(u => u.id === 2);
console.log(user);           // { id: 2, name: "Rohan" }

const missing = users.find(u => u.id === 99);
console.log(missing);        // undefined

console.log(users.findIndex(u => u.name === "Meera")); // 2

find returns the first matching item (or undefined); filter returns an array of all matches.

some and every: yes/no questions

const scores = [72, 88, 45, 91];

console.log(scores.some(s => s < 50));   // true: at least one failed
console.log(scores.every(s => s >= 40)); // true: everyone passed

reduce: boil a list down to one value

reduce combines all items into a single result: a total, a maximum, a count, even an object.

const cart = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, qty: 3 },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250, qty: 1 },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, qty: 2 }
];

const total = cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0);
console.log(`Total: ₹${total}`); // ₹1208

How it works:

  • The function receives an accumulator (sum, the result so far) and the current item.
  • Whatever it returns becomes the accumulator for the next item.
  • The 0 at the end is the starting value.

Round by round: 0 → 360 → 610 → 1208.

Counting things by category:

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", category: "stationery" },
  { name: "Headphones", category: "electronics" },
  { name: "Pen set", category: "stationery" }
];

const counts = products.reduce((acc, p) => {
  acc[p.category] = (acc[p.category] || 0) + 1;
  return acc;
}, {});

console.log(counts); // { stationery: 2, electronics: 1 }

Chaining methods

Because map and filter return arrays, you can chain them into a clear data pipeline:

const products = [
  { name: "Notebook", price: 120, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "Headphones", price: 1499, category: "electronics", inStock: false },
  { name: "Pen set", price: 250, category: "stationery", inStock: true },
  { name: "USB cable", price: 299, category: "electronics", inStock: true },
  { name: "Backpack", price: 1899, category: "bags", inStock: true }
];

const result = products
  .filter(p => p.inStock)
  .filter(p => p.price < 1000)
  .sort((a, b) => a.price - b.price)
  .map(p => `${p.name} (₹${p.price})`);

console.log(result);

Read it top to bottom: in stock → under ₹1000 → cheapest first → formatted labels. (Careful: sort changes the array it's called on. Here that's fine, because filter already made a new array.)

Other handy methods

const nested = [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]];
console.log(nested.flat());                   // [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

const words = ["hello", "world"];
console.log(words.flatMap(w => w.split(""))); // all letters in one array

const nums = [3, 1, 2];
const sorted = nums.toSorted((a, b) => a - b); // sorted copy (modern browsers)
console.log(nums, sorted);

console.log(Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i * 10)); // [0, 10, 20, 30, 40]

Which method do I need?

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting to return in an arrow function with braces: p => { p.price * 2 } returns undefined. Write p => p.price * 2 or add return.
  • **Using map just to loop** and ignoring its result; use forEach.
  • **Forgetting the starting value in reduce**.
  • **Expecting filter to return one item**; it always returns an array.

Exercise

Using the products array from the chaining example:

  1. Get an array of just the product names with map.
  2. Get all electronics with filter.
  3. Find the product called "Backpack" with find.
  4. Check if any product costs more than ₹1500 with some.
  5. Calculate the total price of all in-stock products with filter + reduce.
  6. Produce a list of "NAME – ₹PRICE" strings for stationery, sorted by price.

Summary

  • map transforms, filter selects, find gets the first match, reduce combines.
  • some and every answer yes/no questions about a list.
  • These methods return new arrays (except forEach, sort and reverse), so they chain well.
  • Chained methods turn complex data processing into readable pipelines.

Next, you'll learn objects, the way to group related data with names.
