item.title: JavaScript Objects
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Arrays store ordered lists. Objects store related information under names, like a user's name, email and age, or a product's title, price and stock. Almost all data on the web, from API responses to settings, is made of objects.

Creating an object

const user = {
  name: "Asha Verma",
  age: 21,
  email: "asha@example.com",
  isMember: true,
  skills: ["HTML", "CSS"]
};

console.log(user);

An object is written with braces { } and contains properties: key: value pairs separated by commas. Values can be any type, including arrays and other objects.

Reading properties

const user = { name: "Asha", age: 21, "favourite colour": "teal" };

console.log(user.name);                 // dot notation
console.log(user["age"]);               // bracket notation
console.log(user["favourite colour"]);  // brackets for keys with spaces

const field = "name";
console.log(user[field]);               // brackets with a variable

console.log(user.phone);                // undefined: no such property
  • Dot notation (user.name) is the usual way.
  • Bracket notation is needed when the key is stored in a variable or contains spaces or hyphens.

Adding, changing and deleting

const book = { title: "Atomic Habits", pages: 320 };

book.pages = 322;            // change
book.author = "James Clear"; // add a new property
delete book.pages;           // remove

console.log(book);

Like arrays, a const object can have its properties changed; you just can't replace the whole object.

Nested objects

const order = {
  id: 1042,
  customer: {
    name: "Rohan",
    address: { city: "Pune", pin: "411001" }
  },
  items: [
    { name: "Notebook", qty: 2 },
    { name: "Pen", qty: 5 }
  ]
};

console.log(order.customer.address.city); // "Pune"
console.log(order.items[1].name);         // "Pen"
console.log(order.items.length);          // 2

Read nested paths from left to right: order → customer → address → city.

Optional chaining

If a part of the path might be missing, ?. stops safely instead of throwing an error:

const user = { name: "Meera" };

// console.log(user.address.city);  // TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined
console.log(user.address?.city);     // undefined, no error
console.log(user.address?.city ?? "City not set");

Methods: functions inside objects

const counter = {
  count: 0,
  increment() {
    this.count++;
    return this.count;
  },
  reset() {
    this.count = 0;
  }
};

counter.increment();
counter.increment();
console.log(counter.count); // 2
counter.reset();
console.log(counter.count); // 0

A function stored in an object is called a method. Inside it, this refers to the object the method was called on. You've used built-in methods all along: console.log, "text".toUpperCase().

Shorthand properties

When a variable has the same name as the key, you can write it once:

const name = "Kabir";
const age = 30;

const person = { name, age };   // same as { name: name, age: age }
console.log(person);

Looping over objects

const stock = { pens: 40, notebooks: 12, erasers: 0 };

console.log(Object.keys(stock));    // ["pens", "notebooks", "erasers"]
console.log(Object.values(stock));  // [40, 12, 0]
console.log(Object.entries(stock)); // [["pens", 40], ["notebooks", 12], ["erasers", 0]]

for (const [item, qty] of Object.entries(stock)) {
  console.log(`${item}: ${qty > 0 ? qty : "out of stock"}`);
}

Object.entries plus for...of is the cleanest way to loop over an object.

Checking whether a property exists

const settings = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 0 };

console.log("theme" in settings);           // true
console.log(Object.hasOwn(settings, "lang")); // false
console.log(settings.fontSize ? "set" : "not set"); // "not set": wrong, 0 is falsy!
console.log("fontSize" in settings ? "set" : "not set"); // "set": correct

Destructuring objects

const product = { title: "Backpack", price: 1899, stock: 7 };

const { title, price } = product;
console.log(title, price);

const { stock: available, colour = "black" } = product; // rename and default value
console.log(available, colour);

Destructuring is used everywhere in modern JavaScript, especially for function parameters.

Copying and merging

Objects, like arrays, are stored by reference:

const a = { x: 1 };
const b = a;      // same object, not a copy
b.x = 99;
console.log(a.x); // 99

const original = { theme: "light", size: 16 };
const copy = { ...original };                 // shallow copy
const updated = { ...original, theme: "dark" }; // copy + override
console.log(original, copy, updated);

The spread ... copies the top-level properties. Nested objects inside are still shared; for a full deep copy, use structuredClone(obj).

Arrays of objects

The most common data shape on the web:

const students = [
  { name: "Asha", score: 92 },
  { name: "Rohan", score: 78 },
  { name: "Meera", score: 85 }
];

const top = students.filter(s => s.score > 80).map(s => s.name);
console.log(top); // ["Asha", "Meera"]

Common mistakes

  • Missing commas between properties.
  • Dot notation with a variable: user.field looks for a property literally called "field". Use user[field].
  • Reading deep paths that might not exist: use ?..
  • **Thinking = copies an object**: use { ...obj } or structuredClone.

Exercise

  1. Create an object for a film with title, year, rating and an array of actors. Print a sentence about it.
  2. Add a director property, change the rating, and delete the year.
  3. Loop over the object with Object.entries and print each key and value.
  4. Create a bankAccount object with balance, deposit(amount) and withdraw(amount) methods. Don't allow withdrawing more than the balance.
  5. Use destructuring to pull out the title and rating.

Summary

  • Objects store key: value properties; read them with obj.key or obj["key"].
  • Use ?. for paths that may not exist and ?? for defaults.
  • Object.keys, values and entries let you loop over objects.
  • Destructuring and spread make reading, copying and merging objects easy.

Next, you'll learn functions, the reusable building blocks of every program.
item.excerpt:encoded: Group related data with objects: create them, read and update properties with dot and bracket notation, loop over them, copy them, destructure them and add methods.

item.title: JavaScript Functions
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
A function is a named block of code you can run whenever you need it. Instead of repeating the same lines in ten places, you write them once as a function and call it ten times. Functions make code shorter, easier to read and easier to fix.

Declaring and calling a function

function greet() {
  console.log("Hello! Welcome to VitalStack.");
}

greet();
greet();
  • function starts the declaration, followed by the function's name and brackets.
  • The code inside { } is the function's body.
  • Writing greet() calls (runs) it. Without the brackets, nothing happens.

Parameters and arguments

Functions become powerful when they accept input:

function greet(name) {
  console.log(`Hello, ${name}!`);
}

greet("Asha");
greet("Rohan");
  • name is a parameter: a variable that exists inside the function.
  • "Asha" is an argument: the actual value passed in when calling.

Several parameters are separated by commas:

function introduce(name, city, age) {
  console.log(`${name}, ${age}, lives in ${city}.`);
}

introduce("Meera", "Jaipur", 24);
introduce("Kabir", "Kochi");  // age is undefined

A missing argument becomes undefined.

Returning values

Most functions calculate something and give it back with return:

function add(a, b) {
  return a + b;
}

const sum = add(4, 6);
console.log(sum);              // 10
console.log(add(add(1, 2), 3)); // 6: use the result directly

return does two things:

  1. Sends a value back to wherever the function was called.
  2. Stops the function immediately. Code after return never runs.
function checkAge(age) {
  if (age < 0) {
    return "Invalid age";
  }
  if (age >= 18) {
    return "Adult";
  }
  return "Minor";
}

console.log(checkAge(25), checkAge(12), checkAge(-3));

A function without return gives back undefined.

console.log vs return

A very common beginner confusion:

function doubleLog(n) {
  console.log(n * 2);   // shows the value, but gives nothing back
}

function doubleReturn(n) {
  return n * 2;         // gives the value back to use later
}

const a = doubleLog(5);     // prints 10
const b = doubleReturn(5);  // prints nothing
console.log(a, b);          // undefined 10

Use return when the result is needed by other code; console.log is only for looking.

Default parameters

function createUser(name, role = "student", active = true) {
  return { name, role, active };
}

console.log(createUser("Asha"));
console.log(createUser("Rohan", "teacher"));

If an argument is missing (or undefined), the default is used.

Rest parameters

... collects any number of arguments into an array:

function total(...prices) {
  return prices.reduce((sum, p) => sum + p, 0);
}

console.log(total(100, 250));          // 350
console.log(total(99, 199, 299, 49));  // 646

Object parameters

When a function needs many options, pass one object and destructure it. The order of arguments then no longer matters, and calls are self-explaining:

function formatPrice({ amount, currency = "INR", decimals = 2 }) {
  return new Intl.NumberFormat("en-IN", {
    style: "currency",
    currency,
    minimumFractionDigits: decimals
  }).format(amount);
}

console.log(formatPrice({ amount: 1499 }));
console.log(formatPrice({ amount: 20, currency: "USD", decimals: 0 }));

Function expressions

A function can also be stored in a variable:

const square = function (n) {
  return n * n;
};

console.log(square(9));

Functions are values in JavaScript: you can store them, put them in arrays and objects, and pass them to other functions. That's exactly what you did with map and filter:

function isEven(n) {
  return n % 2 === 0;
}

console.log([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6].filter(isEven)); // pass the function itself, no brackets

A function passed to another function is called a callback.

Hoisting

Function declarations can be called before they appear in the code; JavaScript moves ("hoists") them to the top:

console.log(cube(3)); // 27: works

function cube(n) {
  return n ** 3;
}

Function expressions stored in const can't be used before their line.

Writing good functions

  • One job per function. calculateTotal shouldn't also update the page and send an email.
  • Name it with a verb that says what it does: getUser, formatDate, isValidEmail.
  • Keep it short. If it doesn't fit on your screen, split it.
  • Prefer returning values over changing variables outside the function.
function isValidEmail(email) {
  return email.includes("@") && email.includes(".") && email.length >= 6;
}

console.log(isValidEmail("asha@example.com")); // true
console.log(isValidEmail("asha.example"));     // false

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the brackets when calling: greet instead of greet().
  • **Forgetting return**, then wondering why the result is undefined.
  • **Code after return**, which never runs.
  • Calling a callback instead of passing it: arr.filter(isEven()) calls it immediately; write arr.filter(isEven).

Exercise

  1. Write celsiusToFahrenheit(c) that returns c * 9/5 + 32. Test it with 0, 37 and 100.
  2. Write isAdult(age) that returns true or false.
  3. Write average(...numbers) that returns the average of any number of values.
  4. Write createProfile({ name, city = "Unknown" }) that returns a sentence.
  5. Write capitalize(word) and use it with map on an array of lower-case names.

Summary

  • Declare functions with function name(params) { … } and call them with name(args).
  • return sends a value back and ends the function.
  • Default parameters, rest parameters and object parameters make functions flexible.
  • Functions are values: store them, and pass them as callbacks.

Next, you'll learn the short arrow function syntax used throughout modern JavaScript.
item.excerpt:encoded: Write reusable code with functions: declarations, parameters and arguments, return values, default and rest parameters, and functions as values.

item.title: JavaScript Arrow Functions
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Arrow functions are a shorter way to write functions, added to JavaScript in 2015. You've already used them with map and filter. They're everywhere in modern code, so it's worth understanding them properly, including the one important way they behave differently.

From function to arrow

The same function, written three ways:

// 1. Function declaration
function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}

// 2. Arrow function with a body
const double2 = (n) => {
  return n * 2;
};

// 3. Arrow function with an implicit return
const double3 = n => n * 2;

console.log(double(5), double2(5), double3(5)); // 10 10 10

To turn a function into an arrow function:

  1. Remove the word function.
  2. Put => between the parameters and the body.
  3. If the body is a single expression, remove the braces and return: the value is returned automatically (implicit return).

Parameter rules

const sayHi = () => "Hi!";               // no parameters: empty brackets required
const square = x => x * x;               // one parameter: brackets optional
const add = (a, b) => a + b;             // two or more: brackets required
const greet = (name = "friend") => `Hello, ${name}`; // defaults need brackets

console.log(sayHi(), square(4), add(2, 3), greet());

Many teams always use brackets, (x) => x * x, for consistency. Code formatters like Prettier do this by default.

When you need braces

If the function needs more than one statement, use braces and an explicit return:

const priceWithTax = (price, rate = 0.18) => {
  const tax = price * rate;
  const total = price + tax;
  return Math.round(total);
};

console.log(priceWithTax(1000)); // 1180

Watch out: with braces, nothing is returned unless you write return:

const broken = n => { n * 2 };
console.log(broken(5)); // undefined

Returning an object

Braces after => are read as a function body, not an object. Wrap an object in brackets:

const makeUserWrong = name => { name: name };    // body with a label, returns undefined
const makeUser = name => ({ name, joined: Date.now() > 0 });

console.log(makeUserWrong("Asha")); // undefined
console.log(makeUser("Asha"));      // { name: "Asha", joined: true }

Arrow functions as callbacks

Arrow functions shine when passing small functions to other functions:

const scores = [72, 95, 41, 88, 60];

const passed = scores.filter(s => s >= 50);
const curved = scores.map(s => Math.min(s + 5, 100));
const best = scores.reduce((max, s) => (s > max ? s : max), 0);
const sorted = [...scores].sort((a, b) => b - a);

console.log(passed, curved, best, sorted);

Compare scores.filter(function (s) { return s >= 50; }): the arrow version is easier to read at a glance.

They're also common with timers and events:

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("One second later…");
}, 1000);

The big difference: this

Regular functions get their own this, which depends on how they're called. Arrow functions **don't have their own this**; they use the this of the code around them.

This makes arrow functions perfect inside methods:

const timer = {
  seconds: 0,
  start() {
    const id = setInterval(() => {
      this.seconds++;                 // "this" is still timer: correct
      console.log(`${this.seconds}s`);
      if (this.seconds === 3) clearInterval(id);
    }, 300);
  }
};

timer.start();

If you used function () { this.seconds++ } inside setInterval, this would not be the timer object and the code would break.

But it makes arrow functions a bad choice for methods themselves:

const user = {
  name: "Rohan",
  greetArrow: () => `Hi, I'm ${this?.name}`,       // this is NOT user
  greetMethod() { return `Hi, I'm ${this.name}`; } // this IS user
};

console.log(user.greetArrow());  // "Hi, I'm undefined"
console.log(user.greetMethod()); // "Hi, I'm Rohan"

Rule of thumb:

  • Object methods → method shorthand name() { … }.
  • Callbacks, small helpers, functions inside methods → arrow functions.

Other differences (less common)

  • Arrow functions can't be used with new to create objects.
  • They don't have the old arguments object; use rest parameters (...args) instead.
  • They aren't hoisted: define them before you use them.
const logAll = (...args) => args.forEach(a => console.log(a));
logAll("one", "two", "three");

Readable arrow functions

Short isn't always clear. Name complex callbacks:

const orders = [
  { total: 1200, status: "paid" },
  { total: 300, status: "pending" },
  { total: 850, status: "paid" }
];

const isPaid = order => order.status === "paid";
const toTotal = order => order.total;
const sum = (a, b) => a + b;

const revenue = orders.filter(isPaid).map(toTotal).reduce(sum, 0);
console.log(revenue); // 2050

The last line now reads almost like a sentence.

Common mistakes

  • **Braces without return** → the function returns undefined.
  • Returning an object without wrapping brackets.
  • Arrow functions as object methods, losing this.
  • Overly clever one-liners that are hard to read.

Exercise

  1. Rewrite function triple(x) { return x * 3; } as an arrow function with an implicit return.
  2. Write an arrow function fullName(first, last) that returns a template string.
  3. Write toUser = name => ({ … }) that returns an object with name and createdAt: new Date().toISOString().
  4. Given an array of words, use filter and map with arrow functions to get the upper-case versions of words longer than 3 letters.
  5. Create a counter object whose start() method uses setInterval with an arrow function to count to 5.

Summary

  • (params) => expression returns the expression automatically.
  • Use braces and return for multi-line bodies; wrap returned objects in ( ).
  • Arrow functions use the surrounding this, which is ideal for callbacks inside methods.
  • Use method shorthand, not arrows, for object methods.

Next, you'll learn about scope: where variables can be seen and used.
item.excerpt:encoded: Write short functions with the arrow syntax, learn implicit returns and returning objects, and understand how arrow functions treat this differently.

item.title: JavaScript Scope
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Scope decides where a variable can be seen and used. A variable created inside a function isn't visible outside it; a variable created at the top of a file is visible everywhere. Understanding scope prevents bugs where variables clash, disappear or change unexpectedly.

Global scope

A variable declared outside any function or block is global: every part of the script can use it.

const siteName = "VitalStack";

function showName() {
  console.log(siteName); // can read the global
}

showName();
console.log(siteName);

Globals are convenient, but in a big program any code can change them, which makes bugs hard to trace. Keep globals to a minimum.

Function scope

Variables declared inside a function exist only inside that function:

function calculate() {
  const result = 6 * 7;
  console.log("Inside:", result);
}

calculate();
// console.log(result); // ReferenceError: result is not defined

Each call gets its own fresh variables, which disappear when the function ends. Two functions can use the same variable names without interfering:

function a() { const x = 1; console.log("a:", x); }
function b() { const x = 2; console.log("b:", x); }
a();
b();

Block scope

A block is any code inside { }: an if, a loop, or just braces. Variables declared with let and const inside a block exist only in that block:

const age = 20;

if (age >= 18) {
  const message = "Adult";
  console.log(message);
}

// console.log(message); // ReferenceError

for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
  // i exists only inside the loop
}
// console.log(i); // ReferenceError

This is good: variables live only as long as they're needed.

Why var is confusing

var ignores blocks and only respects functions:

if (true) {
  var leaky = "I escaped the block!";
  let contained = "I stay inside";
}

console.log(leaky);        // works: var leaks out
// console.log(contained); // ReferenceError

And var can be used before its declaration without an error (it's "hoisted" with the value undefined):

console.log(early); // undefined, no error
var early = 5;

// console.log(later); // ReferenceError with let/const
// let later = 5;

The classic var loop bug:

for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("var:", i), 100);
}
// prints 4, 4, 4: all three share one i

for (let j = 1; j <= 3; j++) {
  setTimeout(() => console.log("let:", j), 200);
}
// prints 1, 2, 3: each round gets its own j

These surprises are why modern code uses only let and const.

The scope chain

When you use a variable, JavaScript looks for it in the current scope, then the scope outside it, and so on up to the global scope:

const level = "global";

function outer() {
  const level2 = "outer";

  function inner() {
    const level3 = "inner";
    console.log(level, level2, level3); // can see all three
  }

  inner();
  // console.log(level3); // ReferenceError: can't look inwards
}

outer();

Inner scopes can see outward; outer scopes can't see inward.

Shadowing

If an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as an outer one, the inner one shadows (hides) the outer one inside that scope:

const colour = "blue";

function paint() {
  const colour = "red";   // a different variable
  console.log("inside:", colour);
}

paint();
console.log("outside:", colour); // still blue

This is allowed, but can be confusing. Use different names when you can.

Accidental globals

Assigning to a variable that was never declared creates a global by accident (in non-strict code):

function setScore() {
  score = 100;  // forgot let/const!
}
setScore();
console.log(score); // 100: a global was created

In strict mode, this throws an error instead. Modules and classes are strict automatically; in older scripts, add "use strict"; at the top of the file. And always declare variables with let or const.

Closures: functions remember their scope

A function keeps access to the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. This is called a closure:

function makeCounter() {
  let count = 0;            // private to this counter
  return function () {
    count++;
    return count;
  };
}

const counterA = makeCounter();
const counterB = makeCounter();

console.log(counterA()); // 1
console.log(counterA()); // 2
console.log(counterB()); // 1: B has its own count
console.log(counterA()); // 3

count can't be reached from outside except through the returned function: it's private. Closures are used for private data, event handlers that remember settings, and many library patterns.

Another example: a function factory.

const makeGreeting = greeting => name => `${greeting}, ${name}!`;

const hello = makeGreeting("Hello");
const namaste = makeGreeting("Namaste");

console.log(hello("Asha"));
console.log(namaste("Rohan"));

Common mistakes

  • Using a variable outside the block where it was declared.
  • Accidental globals from missing let/const.
  • **Using var** and getting leaky or shared variables.
  • Shadowing by accident, then changing the wrong variable.

Exercise

  1. Write a function that declares a variable, then try to log it outside. Read the error.
  2. Create a global theme and a function that shadows it; log both.
  3. Run the var vs let loop example and explain the output in your own words.
  4. Write makeMultiplier(n) that returns a function multiplying its input by n. Create double and triple.
  5. Build a createWallet(start) closure with add(amount) and balance() functions, keeping the balance private.

Summary

  • Global variables are visible everywhere; function and block variables only inside.
  • let and const are block-scoped; var ignores blocks, so avoid it.
  • JavaScript looks outward through the scope chain, never inward.
  • Closures let functions remember variables from where they were created.

Next, you'll start working with the web page itself: selecting elements in the DOM.

item.title: DOM: Selecting Elements
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
So far, your JavaScript has mostly printed to the console. Now it's time to work with the page itself. To change anything on a page, you first have to find it. This lesson explains the DOM and the methods for selecting elements.

What is the DOM?

When the browser loads HTML, it builds a tree of objects in memory called the DOM (Document Object Model). Every element, attribute and piece of text becomes an object that JavaScript can read and change.

<body>
  <h1>Title</h1>
  <ul>
    <li>One</li>
    <li>Two</li>
  </ul>
</body>

becomes a tree:

document
└── html
    └── body
        ├── h1  → "Title"
        └── ul
            ├── li → "One"
            └── li → "Two"

The global document object is the entry point. When JavaScript changes the DOM, the browser updates the page immediately.

getElementById

<h1 id="title">Hello</h1>

<script>
  const title = document.getElementById("title");
  console.log(title);
  console.log(title.textContent);
</script>

Finds the one element with that id. Note: no # here, just the name. Returns null if nothing matches.

querySelector: any CSS selector

querySelector accepts any CSS selector and returns the first matching element:

<div class="card"><h2>Card one</h2></div>
<div class="card"><h2>Card two</h2></div>
<input type="email" name="email">

<script>
  const firstCard = document.querySelector(".card");
  const heading = document.querySelector(".card h2");
  const emailInput = document.querySelector('input[name="email"]');

  console.log(firstCard.textContent.trim());
  console.log(heading.textContent);
  console.log(emailInput.type);
</script>

Everything you learned about CSS selectors works here: classes, ids (#title), attributes, :first-child, descendants and more. That's why most developers use querySelector for everything.

querySelectorAll: all matches

<ul>
  <li class="task">Learn HTML</li>
  <li class="task done">Learn CSS</li>
  <li class="task">Learn JavaScript</li>
</ul>

<script>
  const tasks = document.querySelectorAll(".task");
  console.log(tasks.length); // 3

  tasks.forEach((task, i) => {
    console.log(i + 1, task.textContent);
  });

  const done = document.querySelectorAll(".task.done");
  console.log("Done:", done.length);
</script>

querySelectorAll returns a NodeList: a list that supports forEach, length and for...of, but not map or filter. Convert it to a real array when you need those:

<p class="price">120</p>
<p class="price">450</p>
<p class="price">99</p>

<script>
  const prices = [...document.querySelectorAll(".price")]
    .map(p => Number(p.textContent));
  console.log(prices, "total:", prices.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0));
</script>

Searching inside an element

You can call querySelector on any element, not just document, to search only inside it:

<article id="post">
  <h2>Post title</h2>
  <p class="meta">5 min read</p>
</article>
<p class="meta">Footer meta</p>

<script>
  const post = document.getElementById("post");
  const meta = post.querySelector(".meta"); // only inside the article
  console.log(meta.textContent);            // "5 min read"
</script>

This is faster on big pages and avoids grabbing the wrong element.

Older methods

You'll see these in older code:

// document.getElementsByClassName("card")  → live HTMLCollection
// document.getElementsByTagName("p")        → live HTMLCollection

They return "live" collections that update automatically when the page changes, and they don't support forEach. querySelectorAll is simpler and is the usual choice today.

Moving around the tree

Once you have an element, you can reach its relatives:

<ul id="menu">
  <li>Home</li>
  <li id="active">Tutorials</li>
  <li>Blog</li>
</ul>

<script>
  const active = document.getElementById("active");

  console.log(active.parentElement.id);              // "menu"
  console.log(active.previousElementSibling.textContent); // "Home"
  console.log(active.nextElementSibling.textContent);     // "Blog"

  const menu = document.getElementById("menu");
  console.log(menu.children.length);                  // 3
  console.log(menu.firstElementChild.textContent);    // "Home"

  console.log(active.closest("ul").id);               // "menu": nearest ancestor matching a selector
</script>

closest() is especially useful in event handling: from a clicked button, find the card it belongs to.

Always check for null

If no element matches, you get null, and using it causes an error:

const missing = document.querySelector(".does-not-exist");
console.log(missing); // null

// missing.textContent = "x"; // TypeError: Cannot set properties of null

if (missing) {
  missing.textContent = "Found";
}
missing?.classList.add("x"); // optional chaining: does nothing if null

If you see "Cannot read properties of null", check that the selector is spelled correctly and that the script runs after the element exists (remember defer).

Data attributes as hooks

A clean way to select elements for JavaScript is a data- attribute:

<button data-action="save">Save</button>
<button data-action="delete">Delete</button>

<script>
  const saveBtn = document.querySelector('[data-action="save"]');
  console.log(saveBtn.dataset.action); // "save"
</script>

Keeping class for CSS and data-* for JavaScript means a designer can rename classes without breaking scripts.

Common mistakes

  • **Adding # in getElementById**: getElementById("#title") finds nothing.
  • Forgetting the dot in querySelector: querySelector("card") looks for a <card> element.
  • **Using querySelector when you need all matches**, or calling .textContent on a NodeList.
  • Running the script before the HTML exists.

Exercise

Create a page with a heading, three .item paragraphs (one with class featured) and a <ul> of links, then:

  1. Select the heading by id and log its text.
  2. Select all .item elements and log how many there are.
  3. Select only the featured item with a combined selector.
  4. Get the text of every link as an array with spread and map.
  5. From the second list item, log its previous and next siblings.

Summary

  • The DOM is the browser's tree of objects for the page; document is the entry point.
  • getElementById finds one element by id; querySelector finds the first CSS match.
  • querySelectorAll returns all matches as a NodeList; spread it into an array for map/filter.
  • Navigate with parentElement, children, siblings and closest; always handle null.

Next, you'll change the content, attributes and styles of the elements you've selected.
item.excerpt:encoded: What the DOM is, and how to find elements with getElementById, querySelector and querySelectorAll, loop over results, and move around the element tree.

item.title: DOM: Changing Content
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
You can find elements; now you'll change them. Updating text, toggling classes, creating new elements from data: this is how every dynamic interface works, from a "likes" counter to a whole shopping cart.

Changing text

<h2 id="status">Loading…</h2>

<script>
  const status = document.getElementById("status");
  status.textContent = "Ready!";
</script>

textContent sets plain text. Any HTML tags in the string are shown as text, not interpreted, which makes it safe for user input.

Changing HTML

<div id="box"></div>

<script>
  document.getElementById("box").innerHTML = `
    <h3>New section</h3>
    <p>This HTML was added by <strong>JavaScript</strong>.</p>
  `;
</script>

innerHTML parses the string as HTML. It's convenient, but:

  • Never put user-typed text into innerHTML; it can run malicious code (XSS).
  • Setting it replaces everything inside the element, including event listeners on old children.

Attributes

<img id="photo" src="https://picsum.photos/id/10/200/120" alt="Forest" width="200" height="120">
<a id="link" href="#">A link</a>

<script>
  const photo = document.getElementById("photo");
  photo.src = "https://picsum.photos/id/1015/200/120";
  photo.alt = "River in a valley";

  const link = document.getElementById("link");
  link.setAttribute("href", "https://developer.mozilla.org/");
  link.setAttribute("target", "_blank");
  console.log(link.getAttribute("href"));
  link.removeAttribute("target");
</script>

Common attributes are available as properties (img.src, a.href, input.value, button.disabled). For others, use setAttribute, getAttribute and removeAttribute.

Data attributes

<div id="product" data-price="499" data-in-stock="true">Backpack</div>

<script>
  const product = document.getElementById("product");
  console.log(product.dataset.price);    // "499" (always a string)
  console.log(product.dataset.inStock);  // "true": data-in-stock becomes inStock
  product.dataset.price = "449";
</script>

Classes: the best way to change styles

<style>
  .card { padding: 12px; border: 1px solid #ccc; margin-bottom: 6px; }
  .highlight { background: #fef08a; }
  .hidden { display: none; }
</style>
<div class="card" id="c1">Card one</div>
<div class="card" id="c2">Card two</div>

<script>
  const c1 = document.getElementById("c1");
  c1.classList.add("highlight");
  c1.classList.remove("card");
  c1.classList.add("card");
  console.log(c1.classList.contains("highlight")); // true

  const c2 = document.getElementById("c2");
  c2.classList.toggle("hidden"); // adds it if missing, removes it if present
  c2.classList.toggle("hidden");
</script>

Define the look in CSS, and use JavaScript only to add or remove classes. This keeps styling in one place and is easy to change later.

Inline styles

<p id="note">Watch me change.</p>

<script>
  const note = document.getElementById("note");
  note.style.color = "white";
  note.style.backgroundColor = "#2563eb";  // background-color → backgroundColor
  note.style.padding = "8px 12px";
  note.style.borderRadius = "6px";
</script>

CSS property names with hyphens become camelCase. Inline styles are handy for values calculated in JavaScript, like a progress bar width or a position, but use classes for everything else.

Creating and inserting elements

<ul id="list">
  <li>First</li>
</ul>

<script>
  const list = document.getElementById("list");

  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.textContent = "Added at the end";
  list.append(li);

  const top = document.createElement("li");
  top.textContent = "Added at the start";
  list.prepend(top);

  const after = document.createElement("li");
  after.textContent = "Added after the first original item";
  list.children[1].after(after);
</script>
  1. document.createElement("tag") makes a new element (not yet on the page).
  2. Set its content, classes and attributes.
  3. Insert it with append (end), prepend (start), before or after.

There's also insertAdjacentHTML("beforeend", "<li>…</li>") to insert HTML strings without replacing existing content.

Removing elements

<p id="ad">This message will be removed.</p>
<ul id="items"><li>A</li><li>B</li><li>C</li></ul>

<script>
  document.getElementById("ad").remove();

  const items = document.getElementById("items");
  items.lastElementChild.remove();       // remove C
  // items.replaceChildren();            // would remove all children
</script>

Rendering a list from data

This pattern, data in, HTML out, is the heart of every modern web app:

<style>
  .course { border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 8px; padding: 10px; margin: 6px 0; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .course small { color: #64748b; }
</style>
<div id="courses"></div>

<script>
  const courses = [
    { title: "HTML", lessons: 20, level: "Beginner" },
    { title: "CSS", lessons: 20, level: "Beginner" },
    { title: "JavaScript", lessons: 25, level: "Intermediate" }
  ];

  const container = document.getElementById("courses");

  courses.forEach(course => {
    const div = document.createElement("div");
    div.className = "course";

    const h3 = document.createElement("h3");
    h3.textContent = course.title;

    const small = document.createElement("small");
    small.textContent = `${course.lessons} lessons · ${course.level}`;

    div.append(h3, small);
    container.append(div);
  });
</script>

Change the data array and the page follows. Using textContent for each value keeps it safe, even if the data came from users.

Performance tip

Each change to the page can make the browser recalculate the layout. When adding many elements, build them first and insert them in one go:

const fragment = document.createDocumentFragment();
for (let i = 1; i <= 100; i++) {
  const li = document.createElement("li");
  li.textContent = `Item ${i}`;
  fragment.append(li);
}
document.body.append(fragment); // one insertion instead of 100
console.log(document.querySelectorAll("li").length);

Common mistakes

  • **Using innerHTML with user input** (security risk).
  • **Setting style for everything** instead of toggling classes.
  • **Writing style.background-color**; it must be style.backgroundColor.
  • Creating an element but forgetting to insert it.
  • **Expecting dataset values to be numbers**; convert with Number().

Exercise

  1. Create a paragraph and change its text, colour and font size with JavaScript.
  2. Toggle a .dark class on <body> (define the dark styles in CSS).
  3. Given an array of five tasks, create one <li> for each in a <ul>.
  4. Add a class done to every second task.
  5. Remove the last task from the list.

Summary

  • textContent sets safe text; innerHTML sets HTML (never with user input).
  • Change attributes with properties or setAttribute; read data-* with dataset.
  • Use classList.add/remove/toggle for styling; style for calculated values.
  • createElement + append builds new content; remove() deletes it.

Next, you'll make pages respond to the user with events.
item.excerpt:encoded: Change text, HTML, attributes, classes and styles, create and insert new elements, remove elements, and render a list from data.

item.title: JavaScript Events
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
An event is something that happens on the page: a click, a key press, a form submit, the page finishing loading. JavaScript can listen for events and run a function when they happen. Events are what turn a static page into an interactive app.

addEventListener

<button id="like">♡ Like</button>
<p id="count">0 likes</p>

<script>
  const button = document.getElementById("like");
  const countEl = document.getElementById("count");
  let likes = 0;

  button.addEventListener("click", () => {
    likes++;
    countEl.textContent = `${likes} like${likes === 1 ? "" : "s"}`;
  });
</script>

element.addEventListener(eventType, handlerFunction):

  • The first argument is the event name as a string, without "on": "click", not "onclick".
  • The second is the function to run, called the event handler or listener.

Pass the function itself; don't call it:

function sayHi() { console.log("Hi"); }

// button.addEventListener("click", sayHi);   // correct
// button.addEventListener("click", sayHi()); // wrong: runs immediately, once

Common events

The event object

Every handler receives an event object with details about what happened:

<button id="btn">Click me anywhere</button>

<script>
  document.getElementById("btn").addEventListener("click", event => {
    console.log("Type:", event.type);
    console.log("Clicked element:", event.target.textContent);
    console.log("Position:", event.clientX, event.clientY);
    console.log("Shift held?", event.shiftKey);
  });
</script>

event.target is the element that was actually clicked; it's the most-used property.

Live input

<label for="name">Your name</label>
<input id="name" type="text">
<p id="preview">Hello, stranger!</p>

<script>
  const input = document.getElementById("name");
  const preview = document.getElementById("preview");

  input.addEventListener("input", () => {
    const name = input.value.trim();
    preview.textContent = `Hello, ${name || "stranger"}!`;
  });
</script>

The input event fires on every change, perfect for live previews, search-as-you-type and character counters.

Keyboard events

<p>Press any key (click inside the result first).</p>
<p id="key"></p>

<script>
  document.addEventListener("keydown", event => {
    document.getElementById("key").textContent = `You pressed: ${event.key}`;
    if (event.key === "Escape") {
      console.log("Escape pressed: close the popup!");
    }
  });
</script>

event.key gives the key's value: "a", "Enter", "Escape", "ArrowUp".

Preventing the default action

Some events have a built-in browser action: a link navigates, a form submits and reloads the page. event.preventDefault() stops it:

<form id="search">
  <input name="q" placeholder="Search" required>
  <button>Search</button>
</form>
<p id="out"></p>

<script>
  document.getElementById("search").addEventListener("submit", event => {
    event.preventDefault(); // no page reload
    const query = event.target.elements.q.value;
    document.getElementById("out").textContent = `Searching for "${query}"…`;
  });
</script>

Listen for submit on the form, not click on the button. That way, pressing Enter in a field also works.

Event bubbling

When you click an element, the event first fires on it, then bubbles up through every ancestor to document:

<div id="outer" style="padding:20px;background:#e0e7ff">
  Outer
  <button id="inner">Inner button</button>
</div>

<script>
  document.getElementById("outer").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("outer heard it"));
  document.getElementById("inner").addEventListener("click", () => console.log("button clicked"));
</script>

Clicking the button logs both messages. You can stop bubbling with event.stopPropagation(), but you'll rarely need to. Bubbling is actually very useful…

Event delegation

Instead of adding a listener to every item (including items added later), add one listener to the parent and check event.target:

<ul id="todo">
  <li>Buy milk <button data-action="delete">✕</button></li>
  <li>Study CSS <button data-action="delete">✕</button></li>
</ul>
<button id="add">Add task</button>

<script>
  const list = document.getElementById("todo");
  let n = 1;

  list.addEventListener("click", event => {
    const btn = event.target.closest('[data-action="delete"]');
    if (!btn) return;            // the click wasn't on a delete button
    btn.closest("li").remove();
  });

  document.getElementById("add").addEventListener("click", () => {
    const li = document.createElement("li");
    li.innerHTML = `New task ${n++} <button data-action="delete">✕</button>`;
    list.append(li);
  });
</script>

New tasks can be deleted too, without adding new listeners. Delegation is simpler, uses less memory, and handles dynamic content automatically.

Removing listeners and one-time listeners

function onResize() {
  console.log("Window width:", window.innerWidth);
}

window.addEventListener("resize", onResize);
window.removeEventListener("resize", onResize); // needs the same named function

document.addEventListener("click", () => console.log("only once"), { once: true });

Accessibility reminder

Attach click handlers to real <button> and <a> elements. They work with the keyboard automatically. A clickable <div> doesn't.

Common mistakes

  • Calling the handler instead of passing it: addEventListener("click", fn()).
  • **Using "onclick"** as the event name.
  • Listening to the button's click instead of the form's submit.
  • Adding listeners inside a loop to many items instead of delegating.
  • **Forgetting preventDefault()** and wondering why the page reloads.

Exercise

  1. Build a counter with "+", "−" and "Reset" buttons.
  2. Create a textarea with a live "120 characters left" counter.
  3. Make a form that shows the entered email below it on submit, without reloading.
  4. Close a "popup" div when the user presses Escape.
  5. Build a list where clicking any item toggles a done class, using event delegation.

Summary

  • addEventListener(type, handler) runs code when events happen.
  • The event object tells you what happened; event.target is the element involved.
  • preventDefault() stops built-in actions like form submission.
  • Events bubble up, which enables event delegation: one listener on a parent handles many children.

Next, you'll handle forms and validate user input with JavaScript.
item.excerpt:encoded: Respond to clicks, typing and keys with addEventListener, use the event object, prevent default actions, and handle many elements with event delegation.

item.title: JavaScript Forms and Validation
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Forms are where users give you information, and where things most often go wrong: empty fields, typos, the wrong format. In this lesson you'll read form values with JavaScript, validate them, and show helpful error messages, while keeping the form accessible.

Reading values

<form id="profile">
  <label for="name">Name</label>
  <input id="name" name="name" value="Asha">

  <label for="level">Level</label>
  <select id="level" name="level">
    <option>Beginner</option>
    <option selected>Intermediate</option>
  </select>

  <label><input type="checkbox" id="news" name="news" checked> Newsletter</label>
  <button>Save</button>
</form>

<script>
  const form = document.getElementById("profile");
  console.log(form.elements.name.value);   // "Asha"
  console.log(form.elements.level.value);  // "Intermediate"
  console.log(form.elements.news.checked); // true: use .checked for checkboxes
</script>
  • Text inputs, textareas and selects: .value (always a string).
  • Checkboxes and radios: .checked (true/false).
  • form.elements.fieldName finds a field by its name (or id).

For radio buttons, find the checked one:

// const plan = form.querySelector('input[name="plan"]:checked')?.value;

Handling submit

<form id="signup">
  <label for="email">Email</label>
  <input id="email" name="email" type="email">
  <button>Sign up</button>
</form>
<p id="result"></p>

<script>
  document.getElementById("signup").addEventListener("submit", event => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const email = event.target.elements.email.value.trim();
    document.getElementById("result").textContent = `Thanks! We'll write to ${email}.`;
  });
</script>

preventDefault() stops the page from reloading so JavaScript can handle the data, for example by sending it with fetch (lesson 23).

FormData: all values at once

<form id="order">
  <input name="product" value="Notebook">
  <input name="qty" type="number" value="3">
  <label><input type="radio" name="ship" value="standard" checked> Standard</label>
  <label><input type="radio" name="ship" value="express"> Express</label>
  <button>Order</button>
</form>

<script>
  document.getElementById("order").addEventListener("submit", event => {
    event.preventDefault();
    const data = new FormData(event.target);
    const values = Object.fromEntries(data);
    console.log(values); // { product: "Notebook", qty: "3", ship: "standard" }
    console.log(Number(values.qty) * 120);
  });
</script>

new FormData(form) collects every named field. Object.fromEntries turns it into a normal object. A FormData object can also be sent directly with fetch.

HTML validation first

Remember the built-in validation attributes from the HTML course: required, type="email", minlength, min, max, pattern. They work without JavaScript and give you a solid base. JavaScript adds checks HTML can't do, like "passwords must match" or "username already taken", and lets you control the error messages.

Custom validation with clear messages

<style>
  .field { margin-bottom: 12px; font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .error { color: #b91c1c; font-size: 14px; min-height: 1.2em; margin: 4px 0 0; }
  input[aria-invalid="true"] { border: 2px solid #b91c1c; }
</style>

<form id="register" novalidate>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="username">Username</label><br>
    <input id="username" name="username" aria-describedby="username-error">
    <p class="error" id="username-error"></p>
  </div>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="pw">Password</label><br>
    <input id="pw" name="pw" type="password" aria-describedby="pw-error">
    <p class="error" id="pw-error"></p>
  </div>
  <div class="field">
    <label for="pw2">Confirm password</label><br>
    <input id="pw2" name="pw2" type="password" aria-describedby="pw2-error">
    <p class="error" id="pw2-error"></p>
  </div>
  <button>Create account</button>
  <p id="success" role="status"></p>
</form>

<script>
  const form = document.getElementById("register");

  function setError(input, message) {
    document.getElementById(`${input.id}-error`).textContent = message;
    input.setAttribute("aria-invalid", message ? "true" : "false");
    return !message;
  }

  function validate() {
    const { username, pw, pw2 } = form.elements;
    const results = [
      setError(username,
        username.value.trim().length < 3 ? "Use at least 3 characters." :
        !/^[a-z0-9_]+$/i.test(username.value) ? "Only letters, numbers and _." : ""),
      setError(pw, pw.value.length < 8 ? "Use at least 8 characters." : ""),
      setError(pw2, pw2.value !== pw.value ? "Passwords don't match." : "")
    ];
    return results.every(Boolean);
  }

  form.addEventListener("submit", event => {
    event.preventDefault();
    if (!validate()) {
      form.querySelector('[aria-invalid="true"]').focus();
      return;
    }
    document.getElementById("success").textContent = "Account created!";
  });
</script>

What makes this good validation:

  • novalidate on the form turns off the browser's pop-ups so you control the messages. (Keep the HTML attributes anyway; they document intent.)
  • Each error appears next to its field, in text, and says how to fix the problem.
  • aria-invalid and aria-describedby let screen readers announce the error with the field.
  • Focus moves to the first invalid field.
  • The success message uses role="status" so it's announced.

Validate at the right moment

Showing "invalid email" while someone is still typing their first letter is annoying. A friendly pattern:

  • Validate a field when it loses focus (blur) or on submit.
  • Once a field has shown an error, re-check it on every input, so the error disappears as soon as it's fixed.
// field.addEventListener("blur", () => validateField(field));
// field.addEventListener("input", () => {
//   if (field.getAttribute("aria-invalid") === "true") validateField(field);
// });

Using the built-in Constraint API

You can also use the browser's validation from JavaScript:

<form id="f">
  <input id="age" type="number" min="13" max="120" required>
  <button>Go</button>
</form>
<p id="msg"></p>

<script>
  document.getElementById("f").addEventListener("submit", e => {
    e.preventDefault();
    const age = document.getElementById("age");
    document.getElementById("msg").textContent =
      age.checkValidity() ? "Valid!" : age.validationMessage;
  });
</script>

checkValidity() returns true or false based on the HTML attributes; validationMessage gives the browser's message in the user's language.

Never trust the browser alone

Anyone can turn off JavaScript or send data straight to your server. Client-side validation is for a good user experience; the server must always validate again for security.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting .trim()**, so " " counts as filled in.
  • **Using .value on checkboxes** instead of .checked.
  • Comparing numbers as strings ("10" > "9" is false): convert with Number().
  • Error messages only in red colour or only in a tooltip.
  • Relying only on client-side checks.

Exercise

  1. Build a contact form (name, email, message) that checks all fields are filled and the message is at least 20 characters.
  2. Show each error under its field and clear it as the user fixes it.
  3. Disable the submit button and show "Sending…" after a valid submit.
  4. Use FormData and Object.fromEntries to log all values as an object.

Summary

  • Read fields with .value (strings) and .checked; FormData collects everything.
  • Handle the form's submit event and call preventDefault().
  • Show specific, accessible error messages next to each field.
  • Client-side validation helps users; the server must always validate too.

Next, you'll save data in the browser with Local Storage.
item.excerpt:encoded: Read form values, handle submit, validate input with clear error messages, combine HTML validation with JavaScript, and use FormData.

item.title: JavaScript Local Storage
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Normally, everything in a page's JavaScript is forgotten when the page reloads. Web Storage lets you save small amounts of data in the visitor's browser so it's still there next time: a dark-mode preference, a draft message, items in a to-do list.

Note: the Try it Yourself editor runs your code in a secure sandbox where storage is turned off, so the examples below show an error there. To run them, paste them into the browser console (F12 → Console) on any page, or into an HTML file on your computer.

localStorage basics

// Save
localStorage.setItem("username", "Asha");

// Read
const name = localStorage.getItem("username");
console.log(name); // "Asha"

// Remove one item
localStorage.removeItem("username");

// Remove everything this site stored
// localStorage.clear();

console.log(localStorage.getItem("username")); // null: not found

Data in localStorage:

  • Is stored as key–value pairs of strings.
  • Stays after the tab is closed, the browser is restarted, even the computer is restarted, until your code or the user deletes it.
  • Belongs to one origin (protocol + domain + port). Other websites can't read it.
  • Is limited to about 5 MB per site.

sessionStorage

sessionStorage.setItem("step", "2");
console.log(sessionStorage.getItem("step"));

sessionStorage works the same way, but is cleared when the tab is closed, and each tab has its own copy. Use it for temporary things like progress through a multi-step form.

Everything is a string

localStorage.setItem("count", 5);
const count = localStorage.getItem("count");
console.log(count, typeof count); // "5" "string"
console.log(Number(count) + 1);   // 6

Numbers and booleans come back as strings. Convert them when you read them.

Storing objects and arrays with JSON

Saving an object directly gives you the useless string "[object Object]". Convert it to JSON text first:

const settings = { theme: "dark", fontSize: 18, lessonsDone: [1, 2, 5] };

localStorage.setItem("settings", JSON.stringify(settings));

const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("settings"));
console.log(saved.theme);        // "dark"
console.log(saved.lessonsDone);  // [1, 2, 5]
  • JSON.stringify(value) turns objects and arrays into a JSON string.
  • JSON.parse(string) turns it back into an object.

You'll use JSON again with fetch in the next lesson.

Safe helper functions

Storage can fail: the user may have blocked it, the browser may be in a strict private mode, or the saved data may be corrupted. Wrap it in helpers with try...catch:

function save(key, value) {
  try {
    localStorage.setItem(key, JSON.stringify(value));
    return true;
  } catch (error) {
    console.warn("Could not save:", error.message);
    return false;
  }
}

function load(key, fallback) {
  try {
    const raw = localStorage.getItem(key);
    return raw === null ? fallback : JSON.parse(raw);
  } catch (error) {
    return fallback;
  }
}

save("progress", { course: "javascript", lesson: 22 });
console.log(load("progress", {}));
console.log(load("missing-key", { course: "html", lesson: 1 }));

Your app should always work even when storage isn't available; it just won't remember things. (try...catch catches errors so the program doesn't crash; you'll see more of it in the Async/Await lesson.)

Example: remember the theme

Save this as an HTML file and open it in your browser:

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<head>
  <meta charset="UTF-8">
  <title>Theme demo</title>
  <style>
    body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; padding: 24px; transition: background 0.2s, color 0.2s; }
    body.dark { background: #0f172a; color: #e2e8f0; }
  </style>
</head>
<body>
  <h1>Theme demo</h1>
  <button id="toggle">Toggle dark mode</button>

  <script>
    const KEY = "theme";
    const body = document.body;

    function getSavedTheme() {
      try { return localStorage.getItem(KEY); } catch { return null; }
    }

    if (getSavedTheme() === "dark") body.classList.add("dark");

    document.getElementById("toggle").addEventListener("click", () => {
      body.classList.toggle("dark");
      try {
        localStorage.setItem(KEY, body.classList.contains("dark") ? "dark" : "light");
      } catch {}
    });
  </script>
</body>
</html>

Switch to dark mode, reload the page: it stays dark. This is how VitalStack's own theme toggle works.

Example: auto-save a draft

// const textarea = document.querySelector("#message");
// textarea.value = localStorage.getItem("draft") ?? "";
// textarea.addEventListener("input", () => {
//   localStorage.setItem("draft", textarea.value);
// });
// form.addEventListener("submit", () => localStorage.removeItem("draft"));

If the user accidentally closes the tab, their text is still there when they return.

Seeing stored data

In Chrome or Edge: F12 → Application → Local Storage → your site. In Firefox: F12 → Storage. You can view, edit and delete items there, which is very useful when debugging.

What NOT to store

  • Passwords, tokens for important accounts, payment details or any secret. Any JavaScript running on the page (including a malicious third-party script) can read localStorage.
  • Large data (images, big files): it's small and slow. Use IndexedDB for large amounts.
  • Data that must be shared between devices or users: that belongs on a server.

Common mistakes

  • **Storing objects without JSON.stringify** → "[object Object]".
  • Forgetting that values come back as strings.
  • **Calling JSON.parse on null** or corrupted data without a fallback.
  • Storing sensitive information.

Exercise

  1. Save your name in localStorage, reload the page, and read it back in the console.
  2. Store an array of three favourite lessons with JSON and read it back.
  3. Build a page that counts how many times you've visited it.
  4. Make a textarea that auto-saves a draft and restores it on reload.

Summary

  • localStorage keeps strings across visits; sessionStorage only for the tab's life.
  • setItem, getItem, removeItem and clear manage data.
  • Use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse for objects and arrays.
  • Wrap storage in try...catch, and never store secrets.

Next, you'll load data from the internet with fetch and JSON.
item.excerpt:encoded: Save data in the browser with localStorage and sessionStorage, store objects with JSON, handle errors, and remember a user's theme between visits.

item.title: JavaScript Fetch and JSON
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Modern websites constantly talk to servers without reloading the page: loading more posts as you scroll, checking whether a username is free, showing the weather. The fetch() function makes these requests, and the data usually comes back as JSON.

What is an API?

An API (Application Programming Interface) is a set of URLs a server offers for programs (rather than people) to request data. Instead of an HTML page, the server answers with raw data, usually in JSON.

For practice, we'll use JSONPlaceholder (jsonplaceholder.typicode.com), a free fake API made for learning.

What is JSON?

JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for data that looks almost exactly like JavaScript objects:

{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Learn fetch",
  "completed": false,
  "tags": ["javascript", "api"],
  "author": { "name": "Asha" }
}

Differences from JavaScript objects: keys must be in double quotes, strings must use double quotes, and there are no functions, comments or undefined. You convert between JSON text and JavaScript values with JSON.stringify() and JSON.parse(), as in the previous lesson.

Your first fetch

fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1")
  .then(response => response.json())
  .then(todo => {
    console.log(todo);
    console.log(`Task: ${todo.title}`);
  });

console.log("This line runs first!");

Run it and notice the order: "This line runs first!" appears before the data. Network requests take time, so fetch doesn't wait. It returns a Promise, an object representing a result that will arrive later. .then() says what to do when it does:

  1. fetch(url) sends the request and gives a Promise of a response.
  2. response.json() reads the body and parses the JSON, which also takes time, so it returns another Promise.
  3. The second .then receives the actual data.

In the next lesson you'll learn async/await, which makes this read like normal top-to-bottom code. Many developers find it easier; we'll show both styles.

HTTP status codes

Every response has a status code:

Important: fetch only fails (rejects) on network problems. A 404 or 500 still counts as a "successful" response, so you must check response.ok (true for 200–299) yourself:

fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/999999")
  .then(response => {
    console.log("Status:", response.status, "OK?", response.ok);
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`Request failed with status ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
  })
  .then(data => console.log(data))
  .catch(error => console.error("Something went wrong:", error.message));

.catch() handles any error in the chain: network failures and the error we threw.

Showing API data on the page

<style>
  body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  li { padding: 6px 0; border-bottom: 1px solid #eee; }
  .done { color: #94a3b8; text-decoration: line-through; }
</style>
<h3>Tasks from the API</h3>
<p id="status">Loading…</p>
<ul id="list"></ul>

<script>
  fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=8")
    .then(res => {
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
      return res.json();
    })
    .then(todos => {
      document.getElementById("status").textContent = `${todos.length} tasks loaded`;
      const list = document.getElementById("list");
      todos.forEach(todo => {
        const li = document.createElement("li");
        li.textContent = todo.title;
        if (todo.completed) li.classList.add("done");
        list.append(li);
      });
    })
    .catch(err => {
      document.getElementById("status").textContent = `Couldn't load tasks (${err.message}).`;
    });
</script>

Always show a loading state and a friendly error message. Networks are slow and unreliable, especially on phones.

Query parameters

Many APIs accept options in the URL after ?:

const params = new URLSearchParams({ userId: 1, _limit: 3 });
const url = `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts?${params}`;
console.log(url);

fetch(url)
  .then(res => res.json())
  .then(posts => posts.forEach(p => console.log(p.id, p.title)));

URLSearchParams builds the query string and escapes special characters for you.

Sending data with POST

const newPost = { title: "My first post", body: "Hello API!", userId: 1 };

fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/posts", {
  method: "POST",
  headers: { "Content-Type": "application/json" },
  body: JSON.stringify(newPost)
})
  .then(res => {
    console.log("Status:", res.status); // 201 Created
    return res.json();
  })
  .then(created => console.log("Server replied:", created));

The second argument to fetch sets options:

  • method: "GET" (the default), "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE".
  • headers: extra information; Content-Type says the body is JSON.
  • body: the data, as a string (use JSON.stringify), or a FormData object.

(JSONPlaceholder pretends to save it and returns the result with a new id, but nothing is really stored.)

CORS in one paragraph

Browsers only let a page read responses from another domain if that server allows it, through headers. This rule is called CORS. Public APIs designed for browsers allow it. If you see a "blocked by CORS policy" error, the problem is the server's settings, not your JavaScript; you'd need to call that API from your own server instead.

API keys

Many real APIs (weather, maps, AI) require a key. Never put secret keys in front-end JavaScript: anyone can read your page's code. Keep them on a server and have your front end call your own server.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting return** inside .then when chaining, so the next step gets undefined.
  • **Not checking response.ok**: a 404 page gets parsed as data and fails strangely.
  • Using data before it arrives (outside the .then).
  • **Sending an object as body** without JSON.stringify.
  • No loading or error state on the page.

Exercise

  1. Fetch https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users and log every user's name and city.
  2. Show the users as a list on the page with a "Loading…" message.
  3. Add an input where the user types a number 1–10; fetch and show that user's details on submit.
  4. Request a user that doesn't exist (id 999) and show a friendly error.
  5. Send a POST request with a new to-do item and log the response.

Summary

  • fetch(url) makes HTTP requests and returns a Promise; response.json() parses JSON.
  • Check response.ok; fetch only rejects on network errors.
  • Use .then() for results and .catch() for errors; always show loading and error states.
  • Send data with method: "POST", a JSON header and JSON.stringify(body).

Next, you'll write the same code more clearly with async and await.

item.title: JavaScript Async/Await
item.dc:creator: admin
item.content:encoded:
Some things take time: downloading data, waiting for a timer, reading a file. JavaScript doesn't stop and wait for them; it carries on and handles the result later. This is asynchronous code. async and await let you write it in a way that reads like normal, top-to-bottom code.

Synchronous vs asynchronous

console.log("1. Order coffee");

setTimeout(() => {
  console.log("3. Coffee is ready");
}, 1000);

console.log("2. Read the news while waiting");

Output: 1, 2, then 3 after a second. setTimeout schedules the function for later and JavaScript continues immediately. This keeps pages responsive: the browser never freezes while waiting for a slow network.

JavaScript runs one thing at a time. Waiting tasks are handed to the browser, and when they're done, their callbacks are queued and run once the current code finishes. This mechanism is called the event loop.

Promises in brief

A Promise is an object representing a value that isn't ready yet. It's in one of three states:

  • pending: still waiting,
  • fulfilled: finished with a value,
  • rejected: failed with an error.
function wait(ms) {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

wait(500).then(() => console.log("Half a second passed"));

fetch() returns a Promise, response.json() returns a Promise, and many modern browser APIs do too.

async and await

function wait(ms) {
  return new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(resolve, ms));
}

async function makeTea() {
  console.log("Boiling water…");
  await wait(500);
  console.log("Steeping tea…");
  await wait(500);
  console.log("Tea is ready!");
}

makeTea();
console.log("(The rest of the page keeps working meanwhile)");
  • async before a function makes it an async function. It always returns a Promise.
  • Inside it, await pauses that function until the Promise settles, then gives you its value.
  • The rest of the program isn't blocked; only the async function waits.

fetch with async/await

Compare with the .then() version from the last lesson:

async function loadTodo() {
  const response = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos/1");
  const todo = await response.json();
  console.log(`Task: ${todo.title}`);
}

loadTodo();

Each step on its own line, in order. Much easier to read, especially with several steps.

Error handling with try/catch

async function loadUser(id) {
  try {
    const response = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${id}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
      throw new Error(`User ${id} not found (HTTP ${response.status})`);
    }
    const user = await response.json();
    console.log(`${user.name} lives in ${user.address.city}`);
  } catch (error) {
    console.error("Could not load user:", error.message);
  } finally {
    console.log("Request finished.");
  }
}

loadUser(3);
loadUser(999);
  • try { … } runs the code.
  • If anything inside throws an error (or an awaited Promise rejects), execution jumps to catch (error) { … }.
  • finally { … } always runs, which is useful for hiding a loading spinner.

Returning values from async functions

An async function returns a Promise, so the caller must await it too:

async function getUserName(id) {
  const res = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${id}`);
  const user = await res.json();
  return user.name;
}

async function main() {
  const name = await getUserName(1);
  console.log("Name:", name);

  const notAwaited = getUserName(2);
  console.log(notAwaited); // a Promise, not the name!
}

main();

Modern browsers also allow await at the top level of module scripts (<script type="module">), without wrapping it in a function.

Running requests in parallel

await one after another makes requests wait for each other:

async function sequential() {
  console.time("sequential");
  const a = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1").then(r => r.json());
  const b = await fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/2").then(r => r.json());
  console.timeEnd("sequential");
  console.log(a.name, b.name);
}

async function parallel() {
  console.time("parallel");
  const [a, b] = await Promise.all([
    fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/1").then(r => r.json()),
    fetch("https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/2").then(r => r.json())
  ]);
  console.timeEnd("parallel");
  console.log(a.name, b.name);
}

sequential().then(parallel);

Promise.all([...]) starts all the Promises at once and waits for all of them. It's usually much faster when requests don't depend on each other. If any one fails, Promise.all rejects; use Promise.allSettled if you want every result, successful or not.

A complete example: search users

<style>
  body { font-family: system-ui, sans-serif; }
  .card { border: 1px solid #e2e8f0; border-radius: 8px; padding: 10px; margin-top: 8px; }
</style>
<form id="f">
  <label for="id">User id (1–10)</label>
  <input id="id" type="number" min="1" max="10" value="1">
  <button id="btn">Load</button>
</form>
<div id="out"></div>

<script>
  const out = document.getElementById("out");
  const btn = document.getElementById("btn");

  async function showUser(id) {
    out.textContent = "Loading…";
    btn.disabled = true;
    try {
      const res = await fetch(`https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/${id}`);
      if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`No user with id ${id}`);
      const user = await res.json();
      out.innerHTML = "";
      const card = document.createElement("div");
      card.className = "card";
      card.textContent = `${user.name} · ${user.email} · ${user.company.name}`;
      out.append(card);
    } catch (err) {
      out.textContent = err.message;
    } finally {
      btn.disabled = false;
    }
  }

  document.getElementById("f").addEventListener("submit", e => {
    e.preventDefault();
    showUser(document.getElementById("id").value);
  });

  showUser(1);
</script>

Loading state, error state, disabled button while waiting, and safe textContent output: a solid pattern to copy.

Common mistakes

  • **Forgetting await**, so you get a Promise instead of the value.
  • **Using await outside an async function** (in a normal script).
  • Awaiting in a loop when requests could run in parallel with Promise.all.
  • No try/catch, so one failed request causes an unhandled error.
  • **forEach with an async callback**: it doesn't wait. Use for...of with await instead.

Exercise

  1. Write async function countdown() that logs 3, 2, 1, "Go!" with a one-second wait between each.
  2. Rewrite your users list from the previous lesson with async/await and try/catch.
  3. Fetch users 1, 2 and 3 in parallel with Promise.all and log their names.
  4. Add a loading message and a disabled button to your user search.

Summary

  • Asynchronous code lets JavaScript keep working while waiting for slow tasks.
  • Promises represent future values; async functions return Promises.
  • await pauses an async function until a Promise settles; use try/catch/finally for errors.
  • Promise.all runs independent requests in parallel.
